This development may have a more lasting impact on communities along the coastline. Once oil reaches the shore, “not only does the containment becomes that much harder, but basically [the oil] goes into the sediments and the water … and it becomes embedded for years even after the spill has disappeared,” Keskes explained.
The spill also carries numerous health risks for coastal communities, especially those relying on fishing, she added.
Further north in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has also reported an oil spill affecting Qeshm Island and demanded compensation for the environmental damages. The cause of that spill is unknown.
In addition to the ongoing conflict which has seen multiple vessels attacked across the region, the increase in shadow fleets carrying sanctioned oil is exacerbating the danger of environmental damage.
These vessels are “unregulated and often happen to be decrepit” and fall outside the legal chain of liability, Keskes explained. “In normal non-war-related incidents, something like [the Oman spill] happens, you would have to look at the owner of the ship and then their flag and the insurer. But all three are either unclear or just missing.”
This means the response and the hefty cost of damages will fall entirely on the Omani government, she added.
Farida Elsebai contributed to this reporting.

title: Trump keeps saying the US controls the Strait of Hormuz. Does it?
description: Nearly half a year into the US-Iran war, global oil stockpiles are rapidly diminishing as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively stalled and the two powers at the center of the hostilities argue about who controls the critical waterway.
author: Jessie Yeung
content:
Nearly half a year into theUS-Iran war, global oil stockpiles are rapidly diminishing as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively stalled and the two powers at the center of the hostilities argue aboutwho controls the critical waterway.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly insisted that the strait – through whichoil flowsfrom countries like Saudi Arabia and Iraq to the rest of the world – is under US control.
“They don’t have control. We have total control. We own it, and at some point, maybe they’ll do something, and then they get blown away,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “Right now, we’re in a very good position.” And earlier Wednesday, he claimed the US Navy had swept the strait for mines.
But Iran says it won’t reopen the strait fully until the USmeets its conditions.
The reality is far more complicated than Trump’s proclamation of control, experts say – with ships fearing for their safety amid attacks on vessels in the strait, and the ever-looming threat of US-Iran strikes resuming.
The US naval blockade of Iran is still in effect, barring ships from going to or from any Iranian port either inside or outside the strait. This has strangled Iran’s cashflow and closed the strait to Iranian maritime trade.
There is still some traffic going through the Persian Gulf, headed to non-Iranian destinations. But that traffic is still just a fraction of pre-war levels. For instance, only 14 vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday – compared with the roughly 120 ships that used to cross daily before the war.
That’s largely because “few merchant shipping companies and their ships are confident that the US can ensure their safe transit of the strait,” said Carl Schuster, former director of the US Pacific Command’s Joint Intelligence Center.
Those fears are hardly unfounded. At least four vessels belonging to the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked by drones and missiles in the strait last week alone, the company said. And these attacks drive up insurance costs – further deterring shipping companies while the war rages on.
Besides outright attacks, Iran can also harass ships by flying drones overhead and doing “targeted surveillance of merchant shipping,” said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) in a recent advisory.
Since the war began, there have been 54 reports of damage to vessels in the strait, or the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman which sit either side of it, according to UKMTO, a Royal Navy-affiliated body that monitors maritime security and shipping in the region.
There have also been three confirmed total losses of vessels, it said, and 13 near misses.
“Until you can ensure safe use of the strait, you do not have total control,” Schuster said.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Col. Cedric Leighton agreed that neither side has full control right now. “What you’re really dealing with is a standoff here,” he said.
“Because of the proximity of US forces, because of the blockade, and because of Iran’s ability and willingness to at least threaten the use of mines and the use of small boats to harass vessels … neither side is really able to exercise full control over the strait.”
Both the US and Iran have tools in their arsenal to apply pressure on the other and to harness some control over the strait, which normally carries20% of the world’s oil, and an even higher proportion of the natural gas that some nations are critically reliant on.
Iran, lying right on the strait,has the advantage of proximity. It also has a “psychological and political upper hand,” Schuster said, since the disrupted maritime traffic offers them a political and strategic boost.
The strait’s closure has wreaked havoc on global economies and the energy sector, piling pressure on the US to find a solution or guarantee safe passage through the waterway. This pressure could influence the upcoming US midterm elections in November – another thing that could play to Iran’s favor if the new Congress forces Trump to end the war on terms advantageous to Tehran, Schuster said.
And Iran is prepared to bide its time, it seems, with a top adviser to its Revolutionary Guards saying Tuesday that it could “prolong” the war until Trump is out of office.
“We have to attain deterrence so that the enemy never dares to attack us, so we can live with security,” Mohammad Reza Naqditold PBS.
The US still has a clear military and economic advantage, with heavy sanctions on Iranian oil as well as Iranian assets frozen overseas, say experts.
But the US’ military forces in the region “are basically stretched pretty thin, and they’ve been there for quite some time,” said Leighton. That means the US needs to replenish its forces –by,for instance, rotating a new carrier battle group into the region – to increase its leverage inany negotiationswith Iran over the strait.
And, he added, “the US leverage is limited by its staying power.” If the US backs off for any reason or loosens its grip on the blockade, it loses negotiating power and could have less say overthe future of the strait,including which parties will govern it and what new rules are imposed for shipping.
That leaves Trump in a tough spot – at risk of losing leverage and having to make concessions if he pulls out, but under pressure to end the war and bring cost-of-living relief to his constituents ahead of crucial legislative votes, according to analysts.

title: Why officials decided to smuggle Trump out of Turkey with a catering truck and a secret plane
description: By the time President Donald Trump walked onstage at the end of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, the plan to spirit him out of the country was already in motion.
author: Kevin Liptak, Alayna Treene, Holmes Lybrand
content:
By the time President Donald Trump walked onstage at the end of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey, theplan to spirit him out of the countrywas already in motion.
Earlier that day, American officials had come to the president with alarming information. The Iranians knew which luxury chain hotel he’d been staying at in Ankara. They were aware of how his motorcade was moving around the Turkish capital. And they remained intent on killing him — potentially by using a shoulder-mounted missile to take down Air Force One, US officials familiar with the matter told CNN.
The level of detail Iran had been able to ascertain about Trump’s arrangements in the Turkish capital alarmed his team, even though some American officials thought it implausible an Iranian plot to kill him could be successful at the highly fortifiedNATO summit.
The Israeli government had shared the intelligence of the potential Iranian assassination plot with the CIA, one of the officials said. However, the agency, as well as some other Trump officials, viewed the Israeli intelligence skeptically. Some within the CIA had raised questions about the credibility of the intelligence, as well as whether Iran even had such capabilities to carry through such an attack, the official told CNN.
Still, the disclosures led to a dramatically heightenedstate of alert among American officials, according to US officials and others familiar with what happened at the summit. Iran’s threats on Trump’s life, along with three separate assassination attempts in the United States, have long created an uneasy atmosphere for his team.
And so with a solemn face and clutching a binder in his left hand, Trump emerged two hours late to his press conference to declare the conference a major success. But as he’d been throughout the preceding day, Trump sounded preoccupied with Iran’s desire to see him dead.
“The life of a president is very dangerous,” he offered, flanked by three Cabinet members and some senior staff. “It’s a very dangerous profession.”
Trump left the stage a few minutes later. Four minutes after his motorcade pulled away from the presidential complex, headed toward Ankara’s airport, a white catering truck was pulling into place alongside Air Force One.
Devising a way for the president to leave the country safely had become the preoccupation of a small group of senior officials, who spent the morning and afternoon in Turkey assessing their options and updating Trump as he moved between meetings with world leaders, the officials said.
Time did not allow for lengthy deliberation. Trump was scheduled to leave Turkey on the evening of July 8, only hours after details of the specific threat came to light.
In small rooms inside the ornate, heavily fortified Bestepe Presidential Complex, Gen. Dan Caine, the Joint Chiefs chairman who had arrived in Turkey ahead of Trump, marshaled other top officials in coming up with a plan with the Secret Service.
Officials were weighing a number of factors, including the nature of the threat itself. Israel had first alerted the US to a new Iranian plot to assassinate Trump using its proxies, but the information was vague. With the war against Iran then at an inflection point, some officials believed it could be an attempt to influence Trump’s decision-making.
Three US sources familiar with the matter said American intelligence assessments before the trip showed no indication of a new, specific Iranian plot to kill Trump. Instead, officials described a steady drumbeat of chatter about various Iranian actors calling for Trump’s death.
The desire to target Trump was not limited to Iran’s leadership. At the days-long funeral for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, held the weekend before the NATO summit, mourners held signs calling on Iran to kill Trump.
As the summit got underway, more information came to light from US intelligence centered around the potential threat to Air Force One from a missile fired from the ground near the airport, according to a US official.
To some officials, that sounded like a stretch. Security at the NATO summit was extraordinarily tight, even more than is typical for gatherings of world leaders, given the ongoing war with Iran and Turkey’s proximity to the country.
Tens of thousands of Turkish security forces and police officers had descended on Ankara, and temporary cameras were positioned on nearly every street corner. Multiple layers of security surrounded both the summit site and the airport, where leaders from all 32 NATO members were arriving and departing.
It is not clear where precisely the information about the shoulder-fired missile was derived from. US and regional officials said afterward no militants were taken into custody and no evidence of a missile plot was recovered after the president left.
Still, the Secret Service determined in the short timeframe they had that the potential risk — however uncertain — was worthy of taking seriously.
“The threat was serious enough that extreme measures needed to be taken that day,” a US official told CNN. “We wouldn’t have taken those steps otherwise.”
Some security officials believed the best way to safely remove Trump from Turkey was through secretly leaving the country earlier in the day, when the missile threat was first detected, two sources familiar with the matter said.
That idea was dismissed. And Trump maintained his schedule, including meeting with the leaders of Ukraine and Syria before convening his press conference.
It was clear, however, that the threat on his life was creating a measure of mental weight.
“I saw a thing this morning. I’m on every single one of their lists. And so far, I guess I’ve been a little bit lucky,” Trump said during a morning meeting with the NATO secretary general. “But that maybe doesn’t last very long.”
As officials from the Secret Service, the White House and the military were formulating plans to secret Trump out of the country, a separate effort was untaken by Trump himself to explain why he wasn’t taking the $400 million jumbo jet he’d taken to Turkey back to the United States.
TheQatari-donated Boeing 747 had been a major point of pridefor the president, even if some officials wereprivately wary of flying it overseasto a country neighboring Iran.
The flight from Washington had been successful, and Trump proudly beamed at the new aircraft — painted in a new colorway he’d selected himself — when he met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the airport after he arrived.
The old plane, he told his counterpart on the tarmac, was now just the “back-up.”
Yet security officials determined a day later that neither the new plane nor the older, highly recognizable light blue-and-white model would be ideal for Trump to leave on. That, the president quickly recognized, would lead to some uncomfortable questions about why the jet he had insisted was the finest in the world wasn’t making the return journey.
At 3:42 p.m., just before stepping into a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Trump posted online that the new, Qatar-donated jet would be flying to an airbase in Britain to give troops there a chance to tour it.
“Everybody is so excited, and we thought that they should be the first,” he wrote, adding he would be taking the older jet “for old time’s sake.”
In fact, he would be taking neither. The plan concocted by his advisers and the Secret Service would rely on a carefully planned deception that has long been in the playbook for presidential safety.
“The U.S. Secret Service continuously analyzes a wide range of information to guide our protective operations in real time and across every location we secure,” Secret Service Communications Chief Anthony Guglielmi said. “In light of recent assassination attempts and a significant increase in threats against the President, we remain unyielding in our mission.”
The scheme required Trump to board the older Air Force One jet and quickly walk from the main doorway to another exit on the opposite side of the plane, where the white catering truck was waiting.
Turkish Airlines is well-known for its gourmet meals; members of cabin crew don chefs’ toques and white jackets to serve an elaborate spread of dips and mezze, all of which arrive to their planes inside the hydraulic trucks.
This time, however, the catering vehicle was empty, a person familiar with the matter said. US officials had worked earlier in the day on commandeering the truck, without specifying exactly why they needed it, the person said.
Inside the container, which had been cleaned out ahead of time, were Trump; his always-present executive assistant Natalie Harp; his onetime “body man” Walt Nauta, who now serves as director of Oval Office operations; and Dan Scavino, who runs the White House personnel office but has worked for Trump for decades. Secret Service agents were also present.
Oncethe group had been loaded in, a Secret Service agent in a suit rode in the cab next to the driver for the 162-second drive across the tarmac to the smaller C-32A plane.
It’s not clear how, exactly, the manifest for the catering container was devised. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also joined Trump onboard the C-32A for the flight to Mildenhall airbase in Britain.
Left behind on the larger plane were Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, along with many of Trump’s senior aides: top policy adviser Stephen Miller, communications director Steven Cheung, staff secretary Will Scharf, deputy national security adviser Michael Needham and a deputy chief of staff, Richard Walters.
Other staffers, including in the advance and press offices, also remained on the plane, many unaware Trump was not in his forward cabin and, in fact, wasn’t on board at all. They were told to keep their window shades down.
Former Secret Service agent and CNN contributor Jonathan Wackrow said it is not uncommon for the Secret Service to play a three-card monte-esque game when the president travels. “Decoys happen all the time with the president. If you think about every time he gets on a helicopter in Washington, DC, there are three identical helicopters that shell game constantly,” Wackrow said.
Trump this week insisted to reporters it was actually his plane — and not the decoy — that was most at danger departing Turkey, despite no one knowing he was aboard.
Yet there was at least one indication American officials believed both jets faced potential peril. Fighter jets were mustered to accompany both out of the country.

title: Trump’s Iran headaches are mounting
description: The Iran war hasn’t gone well for President Donald Trump since, well, shortly after it began.
author: Aaron Blake
content:
The Iran war hasn’t gone well for President Donald Trump since, well, shortly after it began.
Despite extensive US military attacks and economic pressure, Iran hasn’t felt the need to capitulate to Trump’s demands. And even when there have been ceasefires with favorable terms for Iran, Tehran still didn’t abide by them.
But Trump’s headaches with the war are mounting. And many of them extend beyond the battlefield and the negotiating table.
Some of the recent developments:
And through it all, Iran only appears to begrowing bolder and upping its demands— perhaps believing that its leverage is increasing.
All of the above threatens Trump’s ability to keep prosecuting the war. And these developments add to the costs of a war — now in its sixth month — whose purpose Americans have never been convinced of in the first place. The president insists he’s not feeling the time pressure, but some in his party would beg to differ with the midterms looming.
The plane switch in particular threatens to add a layer of scandal over the already unpopular war. And as much as anything, itundercuts the administration’s claimsto have decimated Iran militarily.
This week we learned that the Trump administration feared a threat from Iran was serious enough that it warranted sneaking the president off Air Force One for his departure from Turkey last month. (CNN reported Wednesday that the threatinvolved a shoulder-fired missile.)
The munitions supply has long been a sleeping giant. CNN has reported that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and other military leaderswarned Trump before the war beganthat the stockpiles could be an issue in a protracted conflict.
Trump seemed to anticipate a much shorter war, lasting four to six weeks or so. But that’s not what he’s gotten. And increasing reports,including from CNN, suggest Caine’s warnings were well-founded and that key munitions are significantly depleted. The US military has exhaustednearly 80% of its interceptors for a key missile defense system, known as THAAD.
The Trump administration has claimed it has plenty of munitions to finish the job in Iran. But that doesn’t address whether the war might cause the US to be so short of critical munitions — which take time to replenish — that it leaves the country exposed or might embolden an adversary like China to try and invade Taiwan.
That’s increasingly a cost-benefit analysis that administration officials will need to consider. But it’s already a dynamic that threatens Trump’s ability to apply pressure on Iran.
A major question, of course, is whether military or administration officials could even prevail upon Trump if they regard the munitions issue as being dire. But there are increasing signs that key figures are growing weary of the war and sending signals that it might be time to ramp it up.
CNN reported last week that Caine has privately made clear to other top Trump advisers that the administrationneeds to find an off-rampfrom the war because the military options on the table to escalate the conflict could backfire, and airpower alone is unlikely to achieve Trump’s objectives.
There are also signs that loyal Trump allies are increasingly concerned about the war costing Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson said recently that “we’ve got to wrap it up,” and Fox News host Laura Ingraham has said the “clock is ticking.” (Indeed, the Guardian recently reported thatmore Iran war skepticism is seeping inon the normally rah-rah airwaves of Fox.) Even cheerleaders for Trump and his war effort like right-wing influencer Benny Johnson have signaled it’s time to move on.
“Foreign wars with no end in sight are always unpopular. They will always be political cancer,” Johnsonposted on Xtwo weeks ago. He added: “End the war. Be done. Refocus on America. Gas, grocery, home prices and immigration. Thats how we win.”
The length of the war also appears to be contributing to another problem for the administration’s ability to keep prosecuting it: fatigue, poor living conditions and declining mental health among the service members tasked with supporting the war effort.
News outletsStars and Stripesand theNavy Timeshave reported multiple attempts by crew members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln to jump overboard. A sailor recently went overboard, CNN reported, before being rescued.
And around 200 family members of Lincoln crew members voiced concerns about the situation — including lack of supplies, food shortages and water contamination — at town halls last week in San Diego. The Lincoln has been deployed since November and hasn’t made a port call in more than 200 days, which Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said is a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.
The US Navy said it takes “every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
But the emerging story epitomizes Trump’s problems.
He seems to regard continuing the war and keeping up the economic pressure on Iran as largely a cost-free endeavor. The US doesn’t have boots on the ground and there aren’t constant stories about troop deaths. Rising gas prices have been the war’s biggest political problem.
But as the situation stretches months beyond when the administration signaled it would end, other problems are seeping in. Some of them make continuing the war more difficult on a practical level, while others suggest the stalemate will keep giving the administration political problems that it — and its allies — have to reckon with.
And given the war was already looking like an albatross and a quagmire – with the midterms less than three months away — these are pretty inauspicious developments.

title: Sailor went overboard from the USS Abraham Lincoln this month as conditions on the ship prompt lawmakers’ demand for answers
description: A sailor went overboard earlier this month off of the USS Abraham Lincoln, three US officials told CNN, amid reports of worsening mental health for crew members on the ship during an extended deployment for the Iran war.
author: Pamela Brown, Ross Adkin
content:
EDITOR’S NOTE:This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. In the US, call or text 988 for help. TheInternational Association for Suicide PreventionandBefrienders Worldwidehave contact information for crisis centers around the world.
A sailor went overboard earlier this month off of the USS Abraham Lincoln, three US officials told CNN, amid reports of worsening mental health for crew members on the ship during an extended deployment for the Iran war.
The sailor was rescued within an hour, according to one of the officials, and was medically evaluated. A different official said that the sailor had gone overboard wearing a life vest and was not injured, adding that the Navy considered the incident a mental health episode.
The sailor had been assigned to an air wing on the ship, the third official said, and was recovered “by an air wing search and rescue helicopter, treated by Abraham Lincoln’s medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care.”
One of the officials described the seas as rough and specified that the incident had occurred on August 3.
The incident of the sailor going overboard, which has not been previously reported, adds to a growing list of concerns about the crew on the ship. Several Democratic lawmakers are calling for answers after concerns were raised by families of sailors aboard Lincoln about the deteriorating living conditions and worsening mental health during the ship’s record-breaking deployment.
Since the Lincoln left its home port of San Diego last November, the aircraft carrier has been deployed for more than 250 days after being redirected to the Middle East to support US operations in the war with Iran, now entering its sixth month. With more than 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard, it has not made a port call in more than 200 days, setting amodern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
The USS George Washington carrier group, which finished a port visit in Vietnam on August 5, is currently headed to the Middle East to replace the Lincoln, a separate US official told CNN. The official said that the swap had been previously planned. It was not immediately clear when the Washington would arrive.
News outletsStars and Stripesand theNavy Timesreported this week that there had been multiple attempts by crew members to jump overboard, citing interviews with sailors and families of those on board who described the impacts of the lengthy deployment.
On Wednesday, Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut and a member of the Armed Services Committee, wrote to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Acting Secretary of the Navy to express “serious concern” about the increasing length of deployments and demand answers about living conditions aboard the carrier.
“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns,” aboard the ship, he said in the letter, as well as “disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months.”
In a statement to CNN, the US Navy said, “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
The first US official said that the Navy’s internal tracking of reports of suicidal ideation on the ship had gone down in recent months, and that the service does not believe there is a correlation between length of deployment and thoughts of self harm.
According to both the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, around 200 family members of Lincoln crew members voiced concerns over mental health and safety conditions to Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and other senior officials during town hall meetings last Thursday in San Diego.
During the town hall, a spouse tearfully told officials that she received a message that same day from her husband saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow,” Stars and Stripes reported, citing one of the attendees.
Among the other concerns raised were reports of a lack of supplies, food shortages, water contamination and mail system disruptions, according toMS NOW, which reviewed audio and video recordings of the meeting.
In one meeting, Vice Adm. Joseph Cahill, commander of Naval Surface Forces, acknowledged the strain on sailors and their families, according to MS NOW, telling families: “We hear you loud and clear (regarding) the impact this has on families, on service members and the long-term ability of us to stand, sustain our forces’ health.”
On Thursday, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said that conditions on the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented” while talking to reporters on a trip to Central America, though he did not specify his concerns with the reporting.
“We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he said. “Some deployments are longer than others, and ?I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it’s incredible.”
Democratic Rep. Mike Levin of California referenced the meeting in a post on X Friday, saying families described “moldy showers, broken toilets, no hot water for weeks, meals that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas.”
“Sailors so worn down that, according to one family member, the ship’s own doctor warned they need to reach port soon or people are going to start losing their minds,” he wrote.
In its report released Tuesday, Stars and Stripes said its interviews with active-duty sailors and family members, as well as “dozens of public social media comments and posts” by crew, described sailors “struggling with exhaustion and declining morale, including reports of suicidal thoughts and at least one instance where a crew member was prevented from jumping overboard.”
The Navy Times also quoted the wife of one serviceman aboard the Lincoln who said her husband had tried to jump overboard during the current deployment.
“He’s scared,” Annabelle Loma told the Navy Times. “He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out, his 13-year career is ruined, just like that. That’s not fair, that’s not right. That’s not what he should be worrying about right now.”
The Navy Times also spoke to the wife of another sailor who told her he had prevented a fellow sailor from jumping overboard in a separate incident.
In an interview with CNN, the journalist who wrote the Navy Times’ report, Natalie Oliverio, said Loma had not heard from Navy representatives in weeks and is “extremely worried and concerned about how her husband is actually doing.”
Oliverio said Loma faces the stresses of having a spouse deployed while raising their three little children, “so not being able to have answers or direction is really challenging right now for her especially.”
Around a month before the reports of service members jumping overboard, CNN’s Pamela Brown spoke to those aboard the aircraft carrier about low morale.
One service member said in July morale was “pretty low” because they hadn’t stepped off the ship in months. “It’s hard on your mental state… It takes a toll on you.”
Massachusetts’ Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton, a Marine veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, described the reports as “horrific” in an interview with CNN’s Laura Coates and said his committee would be conducting an investigation.
“Sadly I’m not surprised. We have a president, a Commander-in-Chief, who’s made fun of troops for mental health issues. We have a secretary of defense who’s more focused on testosterone tests than actually keeping our troops alive,” he told CNN.
“It’s really hard to be excited about that mission (the war with Iran). There’s no one who believes in it right now, and that’s got to be one of the toughest tolls on our troops,” he said.
AJuly CNN pollfound a record-high 73% of US adults say that President Donald Trump hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems, and 67% think Trump’s decisions about military action in Iran have hurt the US.
Armen Kurdian, a retired US Navy Captain who served aboard the Lincoln, told CNN affiliateKFMB, “It’s not uncommon that a strike group experiences somebody wanting to jump overboard or somebody wanting to commit suicide during a deployment.”
“It doesn’t happen every day obviously, but it does happen. So the fact that it’s happening during this deployment is not surprising,” Kurdian said.
In his letter to the Pentagon, Blumenthal said he had “serious concerns about the increasing length of Carrier Strike Group deployments.”
“If the Administration intends to maintain a prolonged military campaign or an elevated carrier presence in the region, it must explain how it intends to ensure today’s operational requirements do not create tomorrow’s readiness crisis,” he wrote, referencing the possibility of additional US naval forces being deployed to the region.
Earlier this year, the USS Gerald R. Ford broke the record for the longest deployment for an aircraft carrier since the Vietnam War – an extended deployment that challenged morale amid an intense few months of combat.
In March, afire broke outin the ship’s laundry department, taking the crew 30 hours to put out. No sailors were injured, but roughly 600 lost access to their bunks due to the damage.
AsCNN reportedat the time, the Navy as a whole faces issues with sailor burnout, according to multiple sources familiar with internal Navy discussions about the issue. Navy aviation personnel, from pilots to maintainers, are leaving the service at a high rate, according to those sources.
Officials at Thursday’s meetings with Lincoln crew family members would not say when the carrier would return home, citing operational security, spouses told the Stars and Stripes.
“The men and women aboard the Lincoln have answered the call to serve their country,” Blumenthal wrote in his letter to the Pentagon.
“The Department owes them not only adequate supplies, maintenance, and support during this deployment.”
This story and headline have been updated to specify the date when the sailor went overboard off the USS Abraham Lincoln after sources provided clarification.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Alex Stambaugh and Ariel Edwards-Levy contributed to this report.

title: Lawmakers leave the VA secretary out of veterans bill discussions: ‘They don’t trust him anymore’
description: A month after House Republicans failed to pass a veterans health bill, lawmakers are meeting behind closed doors to try to get the legislation back on track. But there’s one key person they haven’t invited to the table: Veteran Affairs Secretary Doug Collins.
author: Brian Todd, Adam Cancryn
content:
A month after House Republicans failed to pass a veterans health bill, lawmakers are meeting behind closed doors to try to get the legislation back on track. But there’s one key person they haven’t invited to the table: Veterans Affairs SecretaryDoug Collins.
Collins and his team at the VA have been excluded from recent meetings on Capitol Hill because some senior congressional Republicans and Trump officials blamed him when the planned House vote was abruptly abandoned in July, according to multiple sources who were involved in crafting the legislation.
“His relationship with the Hill directly is garbage at this point,” said one person familiar with the dynamics surrounding Collins.
“They don’t trust him anymore,” another source familiar with the situation said.
The episode underscores how Collins’ standing in the administration has steadily deteriorated over the past several months. A longtime ally of President Donald Trump who previously served in the House before joining Trump’s Cabinet, Collins has confounded those around him with his lackluster engagement on issues like the veterans health bill, spurring widespread speculation over how much longer he’ll remain in the job.
Data shows some veterans wait months to see a therapist for the first time. The VA secretary has his own numbers
Trump is unlikely to fire Collins, at least for now, amid efforts in the White House to minimize upheaval ahead of November’s midterm elections. But Trump officials have increasingly scrutinized Collins’ performance, including tracking his travel and examining the extent of his involvement in key departmental priorities, said the person familiar with the dynamics. Collins’ receding role has prompted speculation he may soon leave the administration of his own accord, the person added.
Resurrecting the legislation, called the “Take Care of America’s Veterans Act,” is also considered key to the midterms. The bill would expand benefits for tens of thousands of veterans – a key constituency for many Republicans in Congress – and passage would be viewed as an important legislative win ahead of the November vote.
The VA, in an email to CNN, denied that Collins worked against the bill’s passage. VA press secretary Quinn Slaven said: “The Trump administration, Secretary Collins and VAbroadly support this bill, and while we believe it could benefit from some amendments, it contains many priorities of the administration.”
Slaven added: “Under the leadership of President Trump, Secretary Collins is proud to work every day to make VA benefits better, faster and easier to use than ever before.”
The White House did not address Collins’ role in GOP efforts to advance the veterans health bill.
In a statement, spokeswoman Olivia Wales said that the VA secretary “is doing a great job and works tirelessly to deliver for our heroic veterans.” Another White House official downplayed the focus on Collins’ travel, contending that Cabinet officials are encouraged to be on the road to “highlight the administration’s accomplishments.”
The White House also forwarded a statement of support from GOP Rep. Jack Bergman, who sits on the House Veterans Affairs Committee and insisted that Collins “has been great to work with” and has “taken action when we bring him difficult issues involving Veterans.”
The veterans health bill would cut billions of dollars in future disability benefits to some veterans suffering from tinnitus and sleep apnea. The money saved from those cuts would pay for another measure that would allow veterans to receive both their retirement benefits and combat injury-related benefits. Veterans are currently allowed to receive one, but not both, of those benefits.
The bill is also aimed at improving access to private sector care, working to cut down wait times for care and providing benefits for the spouses of deceased veterans, even if they re-marry.
Democrats oppose the bill, along with some veterans service organizations including the Veterans of Foreign Wars, Disabled American Veterans, and Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, saying they disagree with the idea of taking away some veterans’ benefits to pay for other benefits.
Other veterans’ advocacy groups like The American Legion and Concerned Veterans for America are in favor of the bill, pointing to all the ways they say it would expand benefits for many of the roughly 9 million veterans enrolled with the VA as well as their families.
The House adjourned for summer recess not long after the legislation was pulled from the House floor ahead of a scheduled vote. But sources say House Republicans are continuing discussions about the bill – without input from Collins.
The VA secretary had initially indicated to Republican congressional leadership that he supported the measure, but then started to subtly work against it, according to two sources familiar with the interactions.
They said he would signal to some lawmakers he wasn’t entirely behind the bill, telling some GOP members he shared their concerns about the legislation. The tension between Collins and the White House and congressional Republicans wasfirst reportedby Politico.
Some of what the legislation aims to accomplish had been proposed during the Biden administration, through the rulemaking process. But a VA press secretary told the website Government Executive in June that that proposal “would need to undergo significant changes” – further baffling Hill staffers about where Collins stood on the issue.
Confusion over Collins’ stance continued into mid-July, sources say, at which point too many House Republicans started to waver in their support. When the bill was pulled, White House officials and Republican House members and staffers grew angry with Collins, the sources said.
“I’ve never seen them so mad,” one source said of some House Republicans. “Their anger was off the charts.”
Sources say senior Republicans complained to the White House about how Collins and Don Bergin, the VA’s assistant secretary for congressional and legislative affairs, dealt with the bill – and that those Republicans do not view Collins and Bergin as honest brokers moving forward.
After Collins’ handling of the legislation that the president and administration have prioritized, one of the sources said: “They can’t decipher or figure out what’s going on in his mind.”
In the midst of the fallout, Collins praised Trump on Fox Business. “He is providing the leadership over the country to say ‘Hey we want to put America first. We want to put our veterans first,’” Collins said.

title: When they didn’t find fraud while testing a voting machine for the Trump admin, this cyber firm faced a wave of backlash
description: The Trump administration abruptly declined to renew a contract for a cybersecurity firm it hired to examine voting equipment in Puerto Rico after the company didn’t echo administration officials’ false claims of voter fraud, the firm’s executives said in their first extensive public remarks on the episode.
author: Sean Lyngaas
content:
The Trump administration abruptly declined to renew a contract for a cybersecurity firm it hired to examine voting equipment in Puerto Rico after the company didn’t echo administration officials’ false claims of voter fraud, the firm’s executives said in their first extensive public remarks on the episode.
After hearing that the firm had found no evidence of vote tampering, allies of President Donald Trump derailed the cybersecurity firm’s work with the government in part by spreading false claims that the firm was funded by liberal billionaire George Soros, according to the firm’s executives and documents they provided to CNN.
A group of “White House-adjacent” Trump allies was “dissatisfied” that “I was not willing to name and shame at that moment and to say, ‘Turns out 2020 was a landslide for Trump. Nobody knew,’” Jason Wareham, CEO of the firm Mojave Research, said this month at the DEF CON cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas.
Mojave Research had no prior experience in testing election systems when the Office of the Director of National Intelligence contacted them in the spring of 2025 as part of the agency’s broader probe into voting equipment. ODNI hired the firm to analyze a specific voting machine made by Liberty Vote (formerly Dominion Voting Systems) that the agency acquired from Puerto Rico. Mojave did the work in six weeks in Wareham’s basement in Reston, Virginia, according to Wareham.
Mojave submitted a report on their findings to ODNI in July 2025, Wareham said, but it has yet to be made public. However, Mojave chief technology officer Manbir Gulati described the findings in detail at DEF CON’s “Voting Village” symposium.
“We found extensive and largely unacceptable weaknesses, but we did not find evidence that those weaknesses were actively exploited or that votes were altered,” Gulati said.
What Wareham’s team found — and didn’t find — in his basement would become a Rorschach test for Trump administration officials focused on election issues. It’s a cautionary tale of how a company that says it wanted to provide the administration with unbiased election security analysis was rejected by a group of officials who still dispute the results of the 2020 election and have Trump’s ear. The Trump administration’s revisiting of the 2020 election has extended to Arizona, where the FBI hasobtained recordsof an audit that confirmed Joe Biden won the state.
After the company made clear what it had found, multiple figures aligned with Trump began to cast doubt on the integrity of Mojave, according to Wareham.
Wareham, a Republican, submitted a declaration in September under the penalty of perjury to the Trump administration to refute the notion that his company was “some form of deep plant meant to ensure the suppression of truth around compromised elections or election systems,” the declaration says.
Reuters has previouslyreportedon Wareham’s declaration and Mojave Research’s tensions with attorney Kurt Olsen, who has repeatedly disputed the results of the 2020 and served as an adviser to Trump in his efforts to undermine faith in that election, but CNN reviewed Wareham’s full declaration submitted to ODNI. The document sheds light on how a faction of Trump allies has aggressively tried to prove the president’s false claims of voter fraud.
Wareham submitted his declaration and financial statements to ODNI to prove he was not affiliated with Soros, who has long been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories about secret levers of power. The next month, Wareham said he received an email, reviewed by CNN, which said that ODNI had issued a “stop-work order” on the contract.
The declaration alleges that Olsen repeatedly inserted himself into a probe of voting equipment begun last year by ODNI under a program known as the Director’s Initiatives Group.
Olsen had no experience in election law prior to the 2020 election, but hegained tractionin Trump’s orbit — and eventually a direct line to the president — for trying to challenge elections in court. The Arizona Supreme Court ordered $2,000 in sanctions against Olsen and his co-counsel after they made false claims about the 2022 Arizona gubernatorial election in their failed effort to overturn that result.
“During many of those interactions and meetings, Mr. Olsen would inform me he was speaking with [t]he President on the election topic and at times seemed to intimate that he spoke on this issue for him,” Wareham’s declaration says. Olsen did not become a special government employee at the White House until October 2025, but Wareham told CNN that Olsen would routinely attend ODNI meetings on election security prior.
After Mojave’s contract ended with ODNI, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard was present in Fulton County, Georgia, in January as the FBI seized records related to the 2020 election.Gabbard’s presence, which she said Trump requested, alarmed election officials from both parties. Olsen drafted the criminal referral to the Justice Department that led to the FBI seizure.
Wareham’s declaration spotlights Olsen’s alleged actions in the months prior to the FBI seizure in Georgia. Discussions involving Olsen and others in his orbit were “hindered by rampant conjecture and assertions made without supporting evidence or documentation,” the document says.
“I lost count the number of times I heard ‘Maricopa County is a crime scene,’” Wareham said in his declaration. Maricopa County is Arizona’s largest county and has been at the center of Trump allies’ false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.
“In total, despite requests and invitations to provide us materials that could be fully integrated into our reporting, we have received little to nothing that would support anything that Mr. Olsen has said or that would allow us to do a primary forensic analysis of sufficient quality that the [Director of National Intelligence] could rely on our conclusions,” the declaration says.
Olsen, now a Justice Department employee, did not respond to multiple requests for comment, nor did the ODNI. The Justice Department had no comment other than to say that Olsen did not join the department until June. The White House referred questions to the ODNI.
Liberty Vote said it would not comment on Mojave’s findings because it had not seen the report Mojave submitted to ODNI, but added that it “is committed to advancing the future of secure American elections.”
How the US voting system prevents fraud
ODNI officials accepted Mojave’s findings, according to Gulati and Wareham. The split within the administration over the Mojave report and the delay over releasing it has undercut efforts to fix the software flaws in the voting equipment, the Mojave executives said.
“What we encountered [were] a lot of competing factions within the government — people who want the boogey man to be out there and are willing to do anything to find it and then people who actually do genuinely care about the issue [of election security],” Gulati added. “There was a huge faction that was like, ‘Mojave doesn’t know what they’re doing. They’re dummies and that’s why they can’t find evidence of compromise.”
Cybersecurity research of election systems has become a fraught exercise after the 2020 election because of the tendency of conspiracy theorists to equate software bugs with voter fraud.
Gulati said he wrestled with the decision to work with the administration, given the risk his research could be weaponized.
“Because their motivations were off, that doesn’t necessarily mean that the idea of looking into election security is wrong or something that shouldn’t be prioritized,” Gulati said, adding that he would rather contribute his security expertise than stay silent. “There have been plenty of pushes for election security efforts both on the left and the right, as there should be.”

title: The Dodgers are playing a different game than the rest of MLB. Their philosophy could shape baseball’s future
description: The Dodgers aren’t content to simply contend. They’re building a super team that cruises from parade to preseason favorites to formidable force every year.
author: Hannah Keyser
content:
“Of course, the Dodgers got their guy.”
That was the prevailing reaction when LA landed the trade deadline’s biggest prize, two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal – an ace pitcher who could be the difference-maker in October when the Dodgers go for a third-straight title.
The trade struck many fans as further evidence that baseball has become, in a word, unfair – a case of the rich get richer. The Dodgers, beneficiaries of a massive TV rights deal which ispartially shielded from revenue sharingand enjoying the major marketing boon that is global superstar Shohei Ohtani, sign all the best free agents (convincing them to defer portions of the payout, a tactic that technically any team can employ) for the most money. They take big swings at the deadline, and no amount of success seems to satiate the chase for rings.
And yet, the financial might shouldn’t have mattered here. Trades are done not with deep pockets but with prospects and audacity. According to different rankings, either the Tampa BayRaysor the MilwaukeeBrewershave the best farm system in baseball. They could have blown the Tigers away with their offer. In other words, as The Ringer put it, “This Time, Teams Could Have Stopped the Dodgers.”
Why they didn’t is something of a Rorschach test for how you feel about the economic structure of the sport.
You could argue the Dodgers are playing at a different level than most other teams. October is often random and rewards mercurial qualities like “getting hot at the right time.” Most front offices, then, are trying to make the postseason as often as possible to increase their chances that, eventually, the stars align – their roster is healthy, the ball bounces their way, and they emerge with a World Series ring. (This is the“win 54% of games”model espoused by Seattle Mariners president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto – a philosophy he had to apologize for saying out loud.)
The expanded postseason field – now at 12 teams – has made this even more viable. Teams don’t have to be much better than middling to sneak into October and hope to ride the variance of tournament baseball to a title. This strategy requires balancing the needs of now with plans to contend next year and three years from now and five years from now.
Streaming now: How America’s pastime became a Japanese tradition
That is not the philosophy coming out of Chavez Ravine, one that is turning the sport on its side.
The Dodgers, clearly, aren’t content to simply contend. They’re building a super team that cruises from championship parade to preseason favorites to formidable force every October. They’re trying to win the World Seriesnow –the future be damned – but then they’ll do that again next year.
Players like Skubal aren’t just about gilding the lily. Skubal is an undeniable- difference maker – in a playoff series. The reality is a single starting pitcher can’t swing a team’s regular season fortunes all that much down the stretch. Skubal will likely make eight to 10 starts over the final two months of the season before becoming a free agent this offseason.
But come October, the importance of depth is replaced by the impact of a top-line starter, who can take the mound more often with the baked-in off days and cement his legacy while chasing down a ring. Skubal is the kind of pitcher who can change a series, change a postseason – and maybe win a title.
Going after those kinds of players constantly is either bold and brash or bad for baseball or the entire point of sports. Critics would say each iterative instance of making some kind ofwin-nowmove is possible because of their financial parachute. They can afford, literally, to take risks both in free agency and in dealing away prospects.
They don’t have to pay Skubal a penny more than any other team would to secure his services for the remainder of this season, but also, they can afford to replace the future production of the prospects they traded away if it comes to that.
Even the most successful small market teams, those that draft and develop so well and find so many ways to wring production out of the margins that they punch far above their weight in the win column, often have to act with more careful consideration for the ramifications.
On the day before the Dodgers acquired Skubal and broke baseball for the umpteenth time, they had a .627 winning percentage,100% odds of making the playoffs according to FanGraphs, and the highest payroll in the sport. Their odds of winning the World Series – a famously finicky task prone to small sample size flukes – were over 25%, one-in-four for one of baseball’s 30 teams.
That day, the last of July, the Brewers had an essentially identical .642 winning percentage, 99.9% odds of making the playoffs, anda bottom-ten payroll. Last year, the Brewers had the best record in baseball during the regular season; they made the playoffs for the seventh time in eight years before being swept by the Dodgers in the NLCS.
Both teams were linked to Skubal as the trade deadline approached. For both, the pursuit of an ace despite their relatively cushy status in the standings represented admirable ambition. The Rays – another small-market perennial contender punching way above their 28th-place payroll to occupy the top spot in the American League – were linked to him as well.
Still, when news broke that Skubal was bound for Hollywood, it felt like the culmination of the inevitable. The Dodgers lost their game against the Red Sox the night before – the first in a seven-game skid – but still the acquisition of Skubal saw their World Series oddsjump more than five percentage points.
The Brewers are an imperfect foil because they, too, have been great – in the regular season. Since the start of 2023, only the Dodgers have won more games. They’ve done this without household names or a big budget. (Consider: theDodgers represent the top two best-selling jerseys in the sportand five of the top 20; the Brewers have one in that echelon, #20.)
Since the deadline, they’ve eked ahead of the Dodgers in the standings. Tonight, they’ll open a four-game series against one another in Los Angeles. Both are still essentially assured a spot in the postseason and yet the Dodgers’ World Series odds remain nearly three times that of the Brewers.
The simple reason is that the Dodgers have more talent. Even this far into the season, with well over 100 games of sample to draw from, the projection systems still believe the Dodgers are the better team.
If you consider playoff usage patterns – leaning heavily on stars and deemphasizing depth – that disparity is even more pronounced.Projections based on that modelingsee the Dodgers as dominating the playoffs even more than they do in the regular season. The Brewers, however, are among the current contenders least suited to October baseball. (And that doesn’t even take into account howthey have struggled against elite pitching while feasting on bottom-of-the-rotation armsin recent seasons.)
Milwaukee reportedly madea compelling offer for Skubal. The problem isn’t a lack of effort; it’s that they couldn’t afford to be reckless. The Dodgers, simply, can.
Whether that’s an issue of team temperament or a sign that baseball needs a salary cap depends on your perspective.
Either way, save your ire for the Tigers, who had playoff odds just over 25% when they decided to deal Skubal and shift focus to the future.
At the time, they professed to still believe they had a shot at October despite trading their toptwostarters. They were right. They’re 6-3 since the deadline and now hold a wild card spot. Their playoff odds are close to 40%.
If they do get in, they’re unlikely to go far. It’s been more than 40 years since their last title and their odds of taking it this year are under 2%.
If they do make it to October, they’re going to wish they had that ace back.

title: Flock rolls out new police auditing and accountability controls following surveillance concerns
description: Law enforcement technology company Flock introduced new safety controls on Thursday, hoping to curb growing scrutiny and fears around surveillance and police misuse of its tools.
author: Clare Duffy
content:
Law enforcement technology company Flock introduced new safety controls on Thursday, hoping to curb growing scrutiny and fears around surveillance and police misuse of its tools.
Flock’s nationwide network of automated license plate readers (ALPR) cameras —mounted along public roads — take images of passing vehicles’ plates, color and other characteristics to feed into a database. Police departments contract with the company to search the database, billed as a tool to help solve crimes.
But astring of recent police officer resignations or arrestsfor alleged abuses of Flock’s license plate reader camera system, including to stalk exes or romantic interests, have added to nationwide concerns among privacy advocates and community members about the technology. Some cities have cancelled their Flock contracts, and some critics have gone so far as tovandalize the cameras.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley was motivated to update Flock’s safety controls after realizing just how many people lack trust in law enforcement.
“I’ve spent a lot of time in the last two years talking to individuals, and a lot of them have said, ‘Well, I don’t trust the police,’ and I go, ‘Why?’ ‘Oh, well, the police have abused their power so many times,’” Langley said in an interview ahead of the announcement. “What’s changed for me is realizing that we have a responsibility, maybe an obligation even, to the communities we serve to set the standard.”
Inside the growing police use and misuse of Flock’s license-plate reader cameras
Flock is now requiring all customers to use its “Audit Assistance” tool by the end of this year. The tool flags abnormal search behavior — for example, by an individual officer. The tool could help address misuse like, for example, the former Milwaukee police officer who court documents showsecretly usedFlock to search the location of his romantic partner 124 times.
When the system detects unusual searches, the user will be locked out of the systempending an administrator review, according to Flock.
The company says that around a third of its agency customers turned on the Audit Assistance before it became mandatory.
“This is designed to intervene before misuse becomes recurring or widespread, rather than simply documenting misuse after the fact,” the company said in a statement.
The company will also require users to input a case number to justify each search, with the exception of “genuine emergencies” that will be automatically flagged for review, Flock says. This feature was previously optional for police departments,and Flock says it must be turned on for all agencies by the end of this year.
Flock is reducing its standard data retention policy from 30 days — a length of time that theACLUand others had raised concerns about — to seven days. However, agencies can adjust that retention period based on state or local policy, the company said. It’s also adding an “evidence mode” feature that will allow agencies to preserve data longer than the retention policy allows when a search is tied to a specific case number.
And the company will give local jurisdictions the option to limit how outside agencies can search data from their cameras; for example, allowing searches related to theft but not to immigration enforcement.
Langley called the misuse of Flock cameras by police officers “completely unacceptable,” adding that building guardrails in the technology can help address surveillance concerns.
While the company’s updates are intended to address potential misuse, Langley said he’d also like to see state regulators mandate more accountability from police. He suggested requiring audits and tools to detect unusual behavior across all technology used by law enforcement and harsher penalties for abuses of power.
Rebuilding trust in the company’s products — and in law enforcement’s responsible use of them — may be crucial for Flock’s business. Some cities thatcanceled contractswith Flock have recentlyinked dealswith competitor Axon.
“Our customers are the community,” Langley said. “Police might pay the bills. Police might make the decisions, but our customer is the community, because that’s who actually receives the benefit of the product.”
CNN’s Eric Levenson and T.M. Brown contributed to this report.

title: DHS cites recent policy shift after not disclosing death of Guatemalan man who had been in custody
description: U.S. immigration officials said Wednesday they didn’t publicly disclose the death of a Guatemalan man who had a seizure at a New Jersey detention center because they weren’t notified he died after they sent him to the hospital.
author: Associated Press
content:
U.S. immigration officials said Wednesday they didn’t publicly disclose the death of a Guatemalan man who had a seizure at a New Jersey detention center because they weren’t notified he died after they sent him to the hospital.
Jose Chajon-Raxon had the seizure July 19, a day after being processed into Delaney Hall, a privately run immigration jail in Newark, the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. DHS officials said Chajon-Raxon was “taken to the hospital and released from ICE custody on July 22.”
The department didn’t say what happened after he went to the hospital, when he died, or whether he was released from the hospital before his death.
“Per ICE policy, when an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur. This is common sense,” the DHS statement said.
This is part of apolicy changeannounced earlier this year in which the agency no longer reports deaths that occur within 30 days of someone’s release from custody. The move rescinds a 2021 policy implemented by the Biden administration.
U.S. Rep. Rob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who has routinely visited Delaney Hall, said the policy change creates a “loophole” where the agency can release someone from its custody and then “claim it has no responsibility to investigate their death or inform Congress and the public.”
“ICE — consistent with the entire ethos of the Trump Administration — is dead set on avoiding public scrutiny and taking any accountability for its failures,” he said.
DHS said in the statement ICE “remains committed to transparency regarding detainee deaths.”
Chajon-Raxon’s death first became publicly known when it was disclosed by Menendez last week following thedeath of another detaineein early August.
He told reporters ICE granted the person a “discretionary release” from custody after they were taken to a hospital and lost consciousness, and the person died shortly afterward. At the time, he did not identify the person.
In recent months, Delaney Hall has been the site offierce protestsby immigration advocates, with demonstrators at times attempting to block vehicles from entering or leaving the facility. Earlier this year, some people held at the jail launched a hunger strike over the conditions, according to Cosecha, an immigrant advocacy group.
The facility is owned by Geo Group,a private prison contractorthat operates multiple detention centersacross the country. The contractor did not immediately respond to email from The Associated Press requesting comment.

title: A passenger jet that came too close to Trump’s Marine One helicopter highlights continuing air traffic control problems
description: A year and a half after a deadly midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people, dozens of safety recommendations have been issued, and some changes were implemented, but problems with aircraft getting too close together persist.
author: Alexandra Skores
content:
A year and a half after a deadly midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people, dozens of safety recommendations have been issued, and some changes were implemented, but problems with aircraft getting too close together persist.
Last Tuesday,planes continued to take off as Marine One lifted off from the Ellipse, just south of the White House, with President Donald Trump onboard. At least one American Airlines regional jet got within the protective bubble around the helicopter. Flights are typically halted from the nearby airport when the President is taking off.
“There was momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another,” the Federal Aviation Administration said, reaffirming the President was never in danger.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Tuesday the breakdown resulted from a telecommunications problem.
“We’ve found at a staff level, between the Marine One team and the FAA, there had been some telecom issues,” Duffy told CNN at a news conference at Newark Liberty International Airport. “We are resolving that, and our teams are working very well together.”
In a recording of air traffic control audio, the pilots onboard Marine One can be heard repeating they will be taking off soon, but the control tower was apparently unable to hear the transmission.
The FAA convened a safety review panel to investigate the incident and agency leadership met with the White House Military Office helicopter unit, the FAA said in a statement on Tuesday.
“While the President was never in danger and the two vehicles were never converging, the group will enhance coordination on three-minute lift notification and boost signal frequencies,” the agency said.
It is the latest in a series of problems at the airport located within sight of the buildings where the nation’s laws are made.
While the incidents are all very different, they illustrate the challenges of managing congested airspace with heightened security, old equipment, staffing shortages, and new legislation aimed at fixing these problems stuck in Congress.
On January 29, 2025,67 people died when an Army Black Hawk helicopter on a training mission and American Airlines regional jet landing at the airport collided over the Potomac River. The deadly crash increased scrutiny of how helicopters are allowed to fly inthe Washington DC airspace.
The National Transportation Safety Board’s final report concluded the crash was caused by a helicopter route too close to where planes were landing, the FAA not regularly evaluating close call data, relying too much on pilots watching for other aircraft, and tower controllers losing situational awareness due to a high workload.
But the problems extended beyond the deadly collision.
In March of last year, an air traffic controller was charged with assault and battery after an “incident” in the control tower. The NTSB revealed in a later hearing that the fight happened as they were in another part of the building investigating the midair collision.
The next day,a close call occurred between a Delta Air Lines Airbus A319 taking off and a flight of US Air Force T-38 jets flying over the neighboring Arlington National Cemetery. A review of tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed the T-38s flying past the airport going more than 350 miles per hour, 800 feet above the ground.
In May of last year, an Armyhelicopter that was instructed to fly over the Pentagon helipadforced controllers to order two flights to abort landings at Reagan National Airport to prevent collisions.
Days later, a congressional hearing revealeda “hotline” between air traffic controllers at the airport and the Pentagon,intended to coordinate aircraft, had not worked since March 2022. The FAA was not aware it was broken until the incident, according to Franklin McIntosh, the FAA’s deputy chief operating officer.
While problems like these can happen at control towers across the country, the deadly collision has put a spotlight on Reagan National Airport, according to Dave Riley, who worked as an air traffic controller for more than 30 years.
“Post the midair, tensions are high,” Riley said. “Scrutiny is extreme. Everything that (Reagan National Airport controllers) say is under the microscope. Everything they do is being scrutinized. So, there’s a lot of pressure there.”
After the deadly collision, NTSB investigators uncovered 15,214 “near miss events” at Reagan National Airport between 2021 and 2024, where aircraft were within one nautical mile of each other, with a vertical separation of less than 400 feet.
During those same four years, there were 85 times where aircraft were less than 1,500 feet apart, and within 200 feet of altitude.
The “data was there” before the crash,Duffy said,but “it wasn’t effectively analyzed to see that we had this kind of risk.”
Close calls between helicopters and planes were not unique to Reagan National Airport.
Last year,the FAA said Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas was identified as having “several immediate issues” with helicopters getting dangerously close to passenger jets.
“All these types of movements around the country are very closely considered,” Riley said. “You try to put those types of helicopters and airplanes in places where they won’t conflict with the regular traffic.”
An AI analysis of safety data led to new nationwide rules requiring helicopter pilots around busy airports be in contact with air traffic control and not rely on looking for nearby planes.
“We identified an overreliance on pilot ‘see and avoid’ operations that contribute to safety events involving helicopters and airplanes,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in March.
Duffy reiterated on Tuesday that “complicated airspaces” like Reagan National Airport will not have helicopters crossing the paths of landing jets.
“Just to be clear, after we had the crash at DCA, we have prohibited cross traffic between helicopters and airplanes, unless it’s presidential movement or if it’s law enforcement or first responder movement,” he said. “But even when that happens, we shut down the airspace.”
Following the January 2025 midair collision at Reagan National Airport, helicopters were also banned from a four-mile stretch of the neighboring Potomac River when flights were landing. So far, this is the only one of the NTSB recommendations stemming from the crash that has been resolved and marked closed by the agency.
NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said more needs to be done.
“We are no closer today to addressing many of the serious safety gaps that contributed to this terrible tragedy,”she wrote in a statement last month.
NTSB investigators formally made 50 safety recommendations in the final report, more than half of which were directed to the FAA.
The agency has testified before Congress that it is working on many of them and has posted a timeline tracking recommendations directed at the FAAon its website.
In addition to the rules prohibiting cross traffic, steps taken include reducing the number of planes allowed to land each hour at Reagan National Airport from 36 to 30, the FAA said. More controllers were also assigned to work in the tower.
“We increased the number of authorized certified professional controllers, support managers, support staff specialists, operations managers and operations supervisors, while simultaneously filling those additional positions,” the FAA said in January.
However, the FAA said not all changes can be acted upon quickly.
“Some recommendations may take several years to implement due to external factors, such as rulemaking and collective bargaining,”the FAA timeline read.
Proposed laws in Congress have also stalled.
The NTSB found “limitations” of “collision alerting systems on both aircraft” contributed to the crash at Reagan National Airport and recommended requiring improvements to the technology and mandates that it be used.
Automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast, or ADS-B, is a radio signal broadcast by an aircraft that includes key location details, including altitude and speed. If a collision is about to happen it can warn a pilot and give them instructions to avoid it.
At the time of the collision, the American Airlines regional jet was sending out a signal, but the Army helicopter that collided with it did not have its system turned on.
Neither pilot was able to receive information, which is part of a newer system called “ADS-B In” that would display nearby aircraft positions for pilots in the cockpit.
A Senate bill, calledthe ROTOR Actwould have required ADS-B In on most aircraft and require most pilots to fly while transmitting ADS-B signals. The bill passed by the Senate, but theHouse of Representatives rejected the measure in February.
A House committee proposed a competing bill, called the ALERT Act, which it says addresses all 50 NTSB recommendations, but would not require ADS-B In on every aircraft.
“Congress has taken significant, historic steps to address many of the Board’s recommendations, and that progress deserves recognition,”Homendy said in July. “But the work is not finished. Congress left for August recess without action on a final bill, and we urge they work through differences during this recess so that a final package can be voted on when Congress returns in September.”
Homendy has warned that without making changes in regulations, operating procedures and laws, close calls and incidents like what happened with Marine One could continue to occur.
“It’s time for action that was promised months ago; we owe it to the victims, to the families who continue to grieve their loss, and to the millions of people who rely on the safety of our aviation system every day,” Homendy said.
CNN’s Pete Muntean contributed to this report.

title: Conspiracies around Nolan Wells’ death have led to threats against those he was with that day, attorneys say
description: On July 4, a group of friends boarded boats and set out from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to celebrate the holiday on nearby Horn Island.
author: Alisha Ebrahimji, Ryan Young, Chelsea Bailey
content:
On July 4, a group of friends boarded boats and set out from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to celebrate the holiday on nearby Horn Island.
It was a trip many had been looking forward to all year, their attorneys would later tell CNN. But it would end in tragedy after Nolan Wells never made it home.
In the weeks since Wells’ body was discovered along the shorelineofthe barrier island, questions around his manner of death have fueledconjecture and fractured a once tight-knit community.
Attorneys representing Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour say despite cooperating with investigators, their clients have effectively become pariahs in their hometown and have been subjected to death threats and defamation.
And, they said, the allegations they were somehow involved in their friend’s death have made it even harder as they try to find ways to grieve the young man they’ve known since middle school.
“The biggest tragedy of this entire thing is that Nolan unfortunately lost his life and nobody knows definitively what happened,” their attorney, Tyler Cox, said, adding all three of his clients have been questioned by authorities in the case.
“These guys haven’t been able to mourn the loss of their friend and brother Nolan Wells,” Cox told CNN Wednesday.
“They left the island at 4:30 pm … So, we don’t know what happened to Nolan after 4:30,” he said. “We want to know just as much as anybody.”
Cox estimates there were hundreds of boats and thousands of people on the island that day. Wells and his friends arrived just before 11 am, he said.
The last time Warren Hudson saw Wells was around 3 pm, his attorneys say.
“They had this little comedic moment because at the time Nolan was kind of holding and cradling a girl that he had met on the island,” Cox said. “You know him being one of Nolan’s best friends, Warren kind of gave him kind of a chuckle, like, ‘Oh, I see you with this girl.’ You know, ‘Hope everything goes well for you.’”
But an hour later, the attorneys told CNN, the group began noticing problems with the bilge pump on one of their boats, the Triton. The water in the hull was rising so quickly it almost covered the battery, and Cox said his clients began to panic and shout to their friends it was time to leave.
What happened next has become the subject of conspiracy and scrutiny.
Cox said there has been an assumption Wells was left “on this deserted, remote island with no access to a phone or no access to anyone else to help him.”
But he was far from alone, the attorney said – and Wells was not the only person who didn’t make the return trip with the group of friends.
“That’s just how it is here. You can always find another ride off the island, and again, there were 2,000 other people there, so he wasn’t left alone by any means,” Cox said.
He also acknowledged many people find it suspicious his clients were in possession of Wells’ phone, but, he said, it’s common practice to drop anchor 50 feet offshore and swim to the island.
“I don’t know anything more corrosive to a cell phone than salt water,” he said. “When they left, not only was Nolan’s phone on the boat, so was five other people’s … and everyone collected the phones after” they got back.
