title: The life-altering choices immigrant families are making under Trump’s crackdown
description: A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for – or avoid – an encounter with immigration authorities.
author: Maria Santana
content:
A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for –– or avoid –– an encounter withimmigrationauthorities.
Some have left the United States after decades of building lives here. Others have considered giving up their unborn child for adoption, so the baby could have a better future.
Parents are naming guardians for their children in case they are detained or deported, while others have stopped working, shopping or even leaving home, relying instead on neighbors and churches.
The choices are deeply personal. Some are irreversible.
Emma Confesor was pregnant with her fourth child when a question she had never imagined began keeping her awake: Would her baby have a better future raised by someone else?
Confesor, 39, emigrated from Puebla, Mexico, more than two decades ago. But uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s effort to endbirthright citizenshipled her to consider placing her unborn child up for adoption.
“It didn’t seem fair to me that the baby wouldn’t have citizenship,” Confesor said through tears. “I had considered adoption so the baby could have a better future.”
For weeks, the possibility consumed her. She said she struggled to sleep, afraid her child could be denied the future she believed every baby born in the United States should have.
Confesor was not alone.
Civil rights groups ask judge to block Trump’s new birthright citizenship order
In an ACLU lawsuit challenging Trump’s executive order, another pregnant woman said she became so desperate to ensure her son would be born a US citizen that she asked her doctor whether labor could be induced early so he would arrive before the policy could take effect. Her doctor advised against it.
Then came the decision that changed everything.
On June 30, the Supreme Court ruled that the 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship, rejecting the administration’s effort to end automatic citizenship for children born on U.S. soil to many noncitizen parents.
For Confesor, the fear that had dominated her pregnancy began to lift.
“I feel relieved,” she said. “I kept thinking, ‘It’s not fair.’ I wasn’t sleeping well because I was worried this could affect me. Not just me, but so many mothers who are going to have babies here.”
While Confesor feared for her baby’s future, other parents were preparing for the possibility that they would not be there to raise their children who were born US citizens.
In Maryland, a Salvadoran mother signed legal papers naming Father Vidal Rivas, the priest at her local church, as temporary guardian of her 7-year-old son if she and her husband were deported.
“It’s not easy to sign a document where it feels like you’re handing your child over to someone else,” she told CNN affiliate Univision through tears.
The uncertainty, she said, had taken a toll.
“I keep thinking and thinking… I feel like my health has suffered because you just don’t know,” she said. “Honestly, I’ve stayed in my house, just praying that God’s will be done.”
She is part of a growing number of immigrant parents making contingency plans in case they are detained or deported.
Many families have already been forced into separation. A CNN investigation published last September found more than 100US citizen children, from newborns to teenagers, had been left without their parents after immigration enforcement actions. Some were taken in by relatives, neighbors or family friends. Others entered foster care.
At St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church in Hyattsville, Maryland, Rivas has been appointed standby legal guardian for at least 31 children whose parents fear they could be detained or deported
“Many of these parents have no other relatives in the country,” Rivas said. “Some want their children to stay here. I would become legally responsible for them so they can continue going to school and have what they need. Other parents hope their children can finish high school before they are sent to reunite with them.”
Rivas said he will serve as a guardian for as long as families need him. “It’s truly as if they were your own children,” he said.
For others, departure has become the only choice that still feels like their own.
Abdiel and Adilene Domínguez had built nearly their entire lives in Minnesota. Abdiel arrived from Mexico at six, Adilene as an infant, and both were protected underDeferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, which grants certain immigrants brought to the US as children temporary protection from deportation and authorization to work, but no permanent legal status.
They married, raised four children, bought a home and opened a church in Minneapolis.
New Trump rule makes it harder for some immigrants to get green cards
But as immigration enforcement increased, they told CNN they became afraid to go to stores or send their children to school. Abdiel also said he was told his commercial driver’s license would be canceled.
Instead of waiting to see what might happen, they sold their home, vehicles and belongings and left for Mexico.
Seven months later, they were living with Abdiel’s mother in Morelos, where the children were struggling with Spanish and enrolling in school, and their parents were trying to adjust to a country that no longer felt familiar.
“I don’t know anything about Mexico,” Adilene told CNN. “Everything I know is Minnesota. I’m in shock.”
The Dominguezes left on their own, without using a federal program. But the pressure they described mirrors a broader Trump administration strategy encouraging immigrants todepart voluntarily.
Project Homecoming, a $915 million initiative, offers free flights and stipends of up to $2,600 to immigrants who leave through the CBP Home app. An internal DHS documentreviewed by CNNin March showed nearly 72,000 people had departed through the program; more than half were already in ICE detention when they enrolled.
More than 72,000 immigration court cases also ended in voluntary departure so far in this fiscal year, compared with more than 35,000 the previous year.
The consequences are also reshaping the lives of US citizens in mixed-status families.
In Pittsburgh, CNN followed Julio Mendoza, an undocumented Mexican immigrant who had lived in the United States since he was 11, as he prepared to leave with his American wife, Sasha, and their three US-born children.
Sasha said they feared Julio could be detained one day and simply not come home. Rather than risk that outcome, the entire family chose to move to Mexico together.
“Everything we do, we do together,” Julio told CNN.
For families who stay, the disruption often unfolds quietly, in the routines they begin to abandon.
Across the country, immigrants have stayed home from work, kept children out of school and avoided stores, churches and other places that once anchored daily life.
Jacobita Cortes, a United Methodist pastor in Chicago, said that fear has changed the rhythms of her community. “They’re afraid to go to the store, to the supermarket,” Cortes told CNN. “Where do our people go? To the supermarkets where you buy your tortillas, your meat; to the church where you go to thank God.”
Some churches, she said, have moved services online, while congregations are helping families who are too afraid to leave home order groceries or arrange school pickups through neighbors and volunteers.
“If someone needs somebody to go do their shopping, they only have to pick up the phone and call,” Cortes said. For parents who are afraid, she added, “find someone who can help, a neighbor or someone who can pick up the children from school.”
The same pattern has surfaced elsewhere. In Minneapolis and New Orleans, CNN found once-bustling shops and restaurants growing quiet during federal immigration operations as some immigrants avoided work and parents kept children home from school.
In Brooklyn’s Little Haiti, normally busy streets and businesses have grown quiet after the Trump administration endedTemporary Protected Status for Haitians.
Community leaders also warned of ripple effects in hospitals, nursing homes and home health care, where many Haitian immigrants work.
For some immigrants, the fear is no longer confined to the possibility of deportation. It is reshaping what it means to live a life in the United States.
CNN’s Carolina Peguero, Priscilla Alvarez, Zoe Sottile, Blake Ellis , Melanie Hicken, Anna-Maja Rappard and Kyung Lah contributed to this report

title: The obsession with ‘Mamdani marts’ isn’t about groceries
description: Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open five government-owned supermarkets in New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media.
author: Nathaniel Meyersohn
content:
Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open fivegovernment-owned supermarketsin New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media.
Taken during Yeltsin’s trip to America months before the fall of the Soviet Union in 1989, the photos show the former Russian president astonished by the variety of frozen foods at Randall’s supermarket in Houston. Yeltsintasted free cheese samplesand surveyed the fish. He left the store with a goodie bag.
On the flight after the impromptu stop, Yeltsin sat motionless with his head in his hands, considering the bare shelves of Soviet food markets. “What have they done to our poor people?”he said, according to his biography.
Then, as now, America’s supermarkets are a marvel of the free market. The idea that government, which has been defined as incompetent and inefficient for decades, could provide grocery abundance and variety better than Walmart and Costco has triggered a visceral reaction among critics. They imagine “Mamdani marts” ending up like dreary state-run Soviet stores with one type of soup.
The response to Mamdani’s plan reflects something much deeper than the brand of ketchup public stores will sell or the price of eggs. It comes down to a fundamental disagreement about the responsibility of government.
Where supporters see government intervening to solve problems of everyday people struggling to afford groceries, others see a socialist mayor overreaching to take aim at a powerful symbol of America’s riches.
“The debate is not really about the specific mechanics of the model,” said Nevin Cohen, an associate professor at the CUNY School of Public Health. It’s a “test of competing ideas about what we expect government to provide.”
Never mind that the public stores aren’t a radical new idea and the city is bringing in private operators to manage them and source the food. Or that 99% of New Yorkers will never shop at one of them. They will not destroy John Castimatidis’ Gristedessupermarket empire.
The American supermarket, with its endless array of products and innovations like theshopping cartand barcodes, has achieved an almost mythical status around the world. Supermarkets helped America project democracy abroad and win the Cold War. For decades, the U.S. Information Agencydistributed imagesof supermarkets to promote the benefits of the “American way of life.”
They are a bounty of consumer choice. Between 1960 and 2010, the number of different products in an average US supermarketgrewfrom 6,000 to 47,000. New business models such as Walmart supercenters, Costco warehouse clubs and Trader Joe’s specialty stores expanded the abundance further.
“Food is a potent symbol and catalyst for people’s politics,” said Tracey Deutsch, a historian at the University of Minnesota who studies food and capitalism. Stores were contested sites duringthe civil rights movementand thepandemic, she noted.
“There’s a sense that grocery stores are the last bastion,” she said. “Grocery stores are places where people make their stand for the world they want.”
Supporters of private sector solutions to address food insecurity say New York City shouldmake it easierfor Walmart to open orpay for Costco membershipsfor people who can’t afford them.
But Mamdani’s animating political philosophy is to use government to solve everyday problems in people’s lives.
He is following in the footsteps of his political idol, Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia, a champion of government intervention during the New Deal who built public parks, housing and the airport that bears his name. Overcoming opposition from private industry, LaGuardiaopened a network of city-run indoor marketsduring the 1930s to move pushcart vendors off streets and reduce the cost of groceries. Several of the markets areopentoday.
Mamdani wants to turn the vacant sites, still owned by the city, into public grocery stores.
LaGuardia “believed in a simple definition of the task of government to make people’s lives better,” Mamdanisaidlast month. “We are one step closer to fulfilling that fundamental responsibility.”

title: Ukraine attacks Russia with hundreds of drones - one of Kyiv’s largest aerial assaults of the conflict
description: Russia says it shot down more than 800 Ukrainian drones overnight in what appears to be among Ukraine’s largest aerial attacks on Russia, with authorities reporting at least six people killed.
author: Tim Lister, Daria Tarasova-Markina, Todd Symons
content:
Russia says it shot down more than 800 Ukrainian drones overnight in what appears to be among Ukraine’s largest aerial attacks on Russia, with authorities reporting at least six people killed.
The two sides have escalated their air war on one another, with Ukraine increasingly firing barrages of drones at targets deep inside Russia, including warehouses and industrial plants as well as refineries.
Russia’s state-run TASS News said it was the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the beginning of the year – with many of the drones targeting the Moscow area where many of Russia’s elite reside.
Air defense forces and electronic warfare units shot down and neutralized 187 drones over the Moscow region, according to its governor, Andrey Vorobiev.
Geolocated video showed a huge fire at a Wildberries warehouse in the Moscow region, the Russian equivalent of Amazon. Vorobiev said no one was injured.
Wildberries’ warehouses have been repeatedly targeted by Ukrainian drones in recent months. Ukraine says it has struck seven out of Wildberries’ ten largest logistics centers. The warehouse struck on Sunday was 250,000 square meters, the Ukrainian military said.
Kyiv has claimed that Wildberries handles supplies for the Russian military, and has stepped up its targeting of other critical parts of the Russian economy.
The company recently announced that it would build new warehousing in neighboring Kazakhstan.
One person, an 83-year-old man, was killed by a drone attack elsewhere in Moscow region on Sunday, according to Vorobiev.
Drones were intercepted over 17 regions – mainly in southern and western Russia – according to the Russian Defense ministry.
Five people were killed in the Rostov region in southern Russia, according to the governor of that region.
A “defense-industrial complex enterprise that produces solid rocket propellant” for various Russian weapons was struck in the attack in Rostov, according to the Ukrainian military.
Russia meanwhile continues to target the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with a mix of missiles and drones.
Six people were wounded by strikes early Sunday, according to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky. A book market in Kyiv was among the sites hit.
Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine were also struck by ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Two people were killed in Kryvyi Rih and another in Sumy in the north, Zelensky said.
Thirteen employees of a steel factory in Kryvyi Rih were injured and one person died, according to Arcelor Mittal, which operates the plant. Rescue and search operations are ongoing, it said.
Ukraine did not shoot down any of the ballistic missiles fired at it overnight, according to an Air Force statement, again highlighting its short supply of missiles interceptors.
Russia fired more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles at Ukraine over the last week, according to Zelensky.
“European interceptors cannot simply be allowed to sit in storage. Lives need to be protected. Russia must be stopped,” he added.
Elsewhere, an unidentified drone was shot down Sunday in Romanian airspace, according to the Defense ministry in Bucharest. The drone was intercepted by a Spanish F-18 fighter jet pilot on a NATO air policing mission.
It was the fourth drone shot down this year over Romania, the defense ministry said.
The ministry said its radars detected the drone entering the country from neighboring Moldova. Fragments appeared to have fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages.
In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace for the first time after dozens of such incursions in the more than four years of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
This story has been updated.

title: How to gauge when to make eye contact
description: Eye contact isn’t just about being polite. It’s fundamental to human connection. But there’s no hard and fast rule about how much eye contact is appropriate.
author: Terry Ward
content:
“Look at me when I’m talking to you.”
It’s a request I heard from my mother throughout much of my childhood, and even into my adult life. Somehow, what has always felt like the right amount of eye contact from my end has often been less than for her.
So many of us have been told to look someone in the eye when speaking. But how much eye contact is the appropriate amount when talking or listening to another person?
There’s no rule, but almost always “people look more while listening than when speaking, although looking is hardly ever just a steady stare,” said Judith Hall, social psychologist and University Distinguished Professor of Psychology, Emerita at Northeastern University in Boston, in an email.
That’s because our eyes are constantly moving around in many small ways when talking or listening. And while people generally have a good sense of when eye contact feels like too much or too little as it’s happening, Hall said quantifying the right amount is not possible.
There are, however, some subtleties to consider.
A guide to mastering small talk with just about anyone, according to experts
It can feel offensive when you’re having a conversation with someone who is averting their gaze. But making eye contact during conversation has functions that go beyond being polite.
“Eye contact isn’t just a social courtesy; it’s actually a brain-stimulating interaction, and it’s really fundamental to human connection,” said Melissa J. Perry, dean of the College of Public Health at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia.
As social beings, humans glean information from others by looking, observing and listening, Perry said. She noted that our brains are “optimized” for seeking out sensory input from others through eye contact and other nonverbal cues, including facial expressions and posture.
Little kids can likely read your emotions even when you wear a face mask, study finds
“Neurobiologically, the brain is responding to the authenticity and empathy and credibility of the person before the mind is forming an opinion about what they’re saying,” Perry added.
Eye contact also has neurochemical effects within the body, including the release of oxytocin, the neuropeptide that plays a crucial role in social bonding, said Paula Niedenthal, a professor of psychology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison whose research examines neural, cognitive, social and cultural/societal influences on facial mimicry and eye gaze.
“The initial function of eye contact is to create a social bond with somebody and to generate activation in the reward systems of the brain and the production of oxytocin to make sure that everybody’s gotten involved in this dance and is going to stay there,” Niedenthal added.
In addition to interacting with the brain’s reward system, eye contact is also important for gathering information.
We learn about people’s moods, behavior and many other things by watching them, Hall noted, whether that’s through direct interactions with people or while watching them without their knowledge.
Making eye contact with someone when they’re talking to you doesn’t have to mean staring right into their eyes, she said. Even people who don’t have difficulty hearing tend to lip-read some during conversation, Hall said, in case you’ve noticed yourself watching someone’s mouth as they talk.
Dogs know if we’re happy, sad or scared just from our expressions, study suggests
When it comes to communicating, more eye contact isn’t always better, Perry cautioned.
“Healthy communication depends on natural intermittent eye contact,” she said. “Too little can suggest uncertainty or disengagement, while too much can feel intimidating or confrontational.”
Averting a gaze during communication can also imply a distance and aloofness, she said, or even a sense of secrecy.
People who consider themselves to be in a dominant position compared with the person they’re talking with have somewhat altered ratios when it comes to how much they make eye contact while speaking and listening, Hall said.
“Their ratio of looking while speaking goes up and their ratio of looking while listening goes down,” she said.
After years of progress on gender, the male gaze is back
There are also differences between men and women. Women are “well established to gaze at others in conversation more than men do,” said Hall, with the highest levels of gaze during communication occurring in pairs of females, and the lowest among pairs of males.
Cultural differences can also come into play when it comes to what’s considered an acceptable amount of eye contact.
“There is a lot of cultural universality although specific cultures can have their own norms,” Hall said. Ethnic groups can vary when it comes to certain situations involving eye contact, too, such as whether sustained eye contact with a superior while talking is considered paying attention or taken as a lack of deference, she said.
Life on the spectrum with Mason
Niedenthal said there’s a “continuum” when it comes to the extent to which eye contact can feel too arousing to different people — another reason there’s no hard and fast rule when it comes to how much eye contact is appropriate in social settings.
People with some neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism, typically avoid eye contact, Niedenthal said.
“The claim is that for those with autism, the high arousal is aversive. Avoidance is thus an adaptive emotion regulation strategy,” she said, noting that it isn’t the only reason why autism is associated with eye contact avoidance.
The best online prescription glasses in 2026, tested by editors (Courtesy CNN Underscored)
If you’re not comfortable with how much someone is looking at you or vice versa, what do you do?
Just being aware of the power of eye contact and other nonverbal forms of communication is a step in the right direction, Perry said.
“It’s far more powerful and impactful than any of us recognize,” she said.
Terry Wardis a freelance journalist and travel writer based in Tampa, Florida, who pitched this story after asking her husband to look her in the eyes when she spoke to him.

title: Democrats adopt 2028 calendar, pushing back Iowa and New Hampshire in favor of more diverse states
description: Democrats on Saturday finalized their 2028 presidential primary schedule, targeting diverse populations that will help shape the party’s fight for White House seat.
author: Fredreka Schouten
content:
Democrats on Saturday adopted a 2028 presidential primary schedule that moves states with sought-after diverse populations to the front of a calendar that will shape their party’s fight to win the White House.
Democratic National Committee members gave final approval to six early voting states, with South Carolina, which has a substantial Black population, continuing to kick off the party’s nominating contests on January 22, 2028.
Nevada, a western presidential battleground, will follow on February 1. The four other early voting states are New Hampshire on February 8, New Mexico on February 15, Michigan on February 22 and Virginia on February 29. The calendar excludes Iowa, a traditional bellwether state for candidates, from the early lineup.
In choosing to include Nevada and New Mexico in the early contests, the party has frontloaded the calendar with states that have large contingents of Latino voters, a group that President Donald Trump made inroads with during the 2024 presidential election.
In an interview with CNN, DNC Chair Ken Martin hailed the calendar as “the most diverse” in the party’s history.
“It’s going to battle-test our nominee with key parts of our coalition and key parts of the country in a way that we’ve never seen before,” he said.
The vote, on the final day of the DNC’s summer meeting, comes amid a midterm primary election season that has seen Democratic voters swing betweenprogressive insurgentsandmoderate candidates— an internal struggle over the party’s direction that likely will loom over the crowded race for the White House.
Martin, who has facedcriticism of his leadershipof the DNC and stewardship of its finances, insisted that those ideological differences should not divide Democrats as they barrel toward this November’s high-stakes midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
“We are a big tent party,” the party chief told a gathering of the DNC women’s caucus on the opening day of the meeting Thursday. “And as long as I’m the chair, we’re going to continue to be.”
“Everybody is welcomed in this party,” Martin said to strong applause and hoots of approval from those assembled in a ballroom at a Hilton hotel in downtown Austin.
Before the vote, party officials from Iowa — which has long held the first nominating contest — made known their displeasure with the new calendar.
“We need a Midwest and a truly rural state to be among the first four states if we hope to build sustainable and lasting majorities that enact real and meaningful change,” Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart argued, urging DNC members to reject the calendar.
In the end, the new schedule passed on a voice vote, prompting sustained applause from the DNC crowd.
In addition to keeping Iowa out of the early state lineup, the committee members pushed New Hampshire deeper into the calendar, though that could also cause some internal party tensions. New Hampshire law requires the state’s top election official to schedule a primary at least seven days before another state carries out a primary.
Proponents of the new schedule say the calendar shake-up will help Democrats engage with the voters the party needs to win the presidential election. Nevada and Michigan both have large amounts of union members, and have substantial numbers of Black voters. And New Mexico’s inclusion puts a heavily Latino and rural border state into the mix.
“New Mexico looks a lot like the America Democrats need to win,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, a Democrat from the state, told CNN in an interview before the final vote. “When our presidential candidates come and listen to and inspire our Latino voters, Latinos across the country are going to understand that they are not being taken for granted.”
The DNC gathering occurred during a time of internal strife for the national party, with some members criticizing Martin’s management decisions and voicing alarm over the national party’s financial health.
The DNC has raised $207 million so far in this cycle — compared with nearly $279 million collected by the Republican National Committee, according to Federal Election Commission filings. But the Democratic committee lags far behind its Republican counterpart in available resources less than three months before the midterms. The DNC ended June with $2 million in debt, while the RNC had nearly $129 million remaining in the bank, FEC filings show.
Martin defended his record. During an interview with CNN, he pointed to a string of electoral victories for Democrats around the country in recent months as an outgrowth of his decision to invest in a permanent campaign infrastructure.
“By every objective measure on how to measure a party — and certainly party leadership — I’m succeeding,” Martin said.
Asked about a report in The New York Times that the party has urged vendors todelay sending invoicesuntil after the midterms to help alleviate the cash crunch, Martin told CNN it was “standard practice” to renegotiate vendor contracts “to make sure you can meet cash flow and keep those relationships intact.”
Martin, who was elected chair early last year, has defenders in the DNC, including among state party chairs who have benefited from the national party’s new investments in their work.
(Last year, the DNC increased the amount it sends to state parties. Blue states began receiving an additional $5,000 a month, for a total of $17,500, and red states got a boost of $10,000 a month, for a total of $22,500.)
“There is no appetite for his removal,” Michael Kapp, a DNC member from California, said flatly. “He’s doing exactly what we asked him to do: building up state parties, investing in training and organizing programs, investing in partisan voter registration and not hoarding our cash.”
Daniele Monroe-Moreno, who chairs the Nevada Democratic Party, said Martin’s investment strategy is making a difference for Democrats in her state, who hope to flip the governor’s mansion and an open US House seat this fall.
“Money’s nice in the bank,” she said, “but I’d rather have the money on the ground doing the organizing.”
Over the course of the gathering, top Democrats exhorted members to stay focused on winning races this fall, rather than party infighting.
“Nobody sitting in Danville, Virginia, right now at their kitchen table worrying about paying their heating bills or groceries is worried about what’s going on at the DNC headquarters, I promise you all that,” former Virginia Gov. Terry McAuliffe, who has also been a DNC chairman, told the gathering on Saturday.
“We need to be unified,” McAuliffe said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Arit John contributed to this report.

title: One Cooper Flagg card changed this collector’s life in an instant
description: Jason Williams landed the one-of-a-kind Cooper Flagg NBA debut patch card — and now has multimillion-dollar offers on the table.
author: Andy Scholes
content:
Jason Williams landed the one-of-a-kindCooper FlaggNBA debut patch card — and now has multimillion-dollar offers on the table.
Williams, a machine shop owner from Clover, South Carolina, suddenly finds himself holding one of the most coveted cards in thesports memorabilia world.
The father of five entered a break of Topps Chrome Update Basketball on Monday and landed the one-of-one Cooper Flagg debut patch card, which has already drawn several multimillion-dollar offers.
Williams told CNN the moment he realized the card was his was surreal.
“When it happened, I mean, I went to the floor like a baby in the fetal position,” Williams said. “I mean, it was just emotional because I knew. I knew what had happened. It took me a few seconds for it to register in my mind, but it was just emotions took over me.”
A “break” is a popular way for collectors to buysports cardswithout purchasing an entire box. Typically conducted via livestream, participants purchase the rights to a specific team or player and receive the eligible cards pulled for that team or player from a set number of packs or boxes.
Williams paid $515 for the Dallas Mavericks in a break conducted by Rhody Breakers, based in Rhode Island.
“I was watching it on my phone sitting in the living room,” Williams said. “My 12-year old was getting ready to go to bed. We knew a card that was coming was gonna be a pretty big one. And I knew I had a big team in that break.”
Flagg’s card is one-of-a-kind and features a patch from the jersey he wore in his NBA debut.
As the breaker got closer to revealing the highly sought-after card, Williams decided to move the livestream from his phone to a bigger screen.
“I was like, ‘hey, we need to put this on the big screen’ and my wife was like, ‘OK, whatever, do what you need to do,’” Williams said. “So I put it on.”
Then the card collectors around the hobby had been chasing appeared on the screen.
It belonged to Williams.
“It was intense,” he said.
Williams, who turned 50 in July, said he has collected sports cards on and off since he was 12. He has long enjoyed opening packs himself but discovered online breaks about six years ago.
“It was totally new to me when I’ve seen it, and I’m old school, so the internet stuff I ain’t really into. But this one I figured out, and it was an easy way to do it,” Williams said. “And this one was a $515 break, so it was an expensive one to me, but well worth it.”
Williams said the adrenaline was so intense that he didn’t sleep that night.
“I got in my truck and I drove to the store and got me a Monster Energy drink,” Williams said. “I knew I wasn’t going to sleep that night.”
Instead, Williams stayed up talking with others in the online chat before going to work at 5 a.m.
“I had to just get my mind off of it, but the excitement level and the adrenaline was so intense that, I mean, I don’t even know how to explain that,” he said.
Pittsburgh Pirates offer outrageous trade for one-of-a-kind Paul Skenes baseball card
Now Williams has another decision to make: What does he do with the card?
The Dallas Mavericks have offered lower-level season tickets for 32 years and a package of other perks in exchange for the card. There are also multimillion-dollar offers from others interested in acquiring it.
For now, he says he’s in no rush to make a deal.
“Right now, I’m not even looking at the money,” Williams said.
“For me, I am looking forward to the experiences that I’m gonna get out of this and the things that my family and my kids are going to get to experience that are memories for a lifetime.”

title: New premium airplane seats have a big problem — and it could be getting worse
description: Airlines are building business-class suites so complex and customized that safety regulators can’t approve them in time — potentially leaving brand-new cabins flying empty.
author: Edward Russell
content:
Imagine booking a ticket on one of Europe’s premier airlines, stepping onto a brand-new, ultra-modern Airbus A350, and walking past 34 of the grandest business-class suites in the sky — only to be told no one is allowed to sit in them.
That ironic reality may await passengers on KLM’s new Amsterdam-Toronto route this fall, among other major carriers. The luxury pods — complete with lie-flat beds and sliding privacy doors — could be entirely off-limits when departure day rolls around, sitting completely empty at 35,000 feet.
The culprit isn’t a lack of demand, but a paradox of modern aviation. As premium seats have become increasingly complex, getting regulatory clearance to fly them is harder than ever, creating a production bottleneck that is about to become visible in the sky.
And it’s not just affecting KLM. Airlines around the world are currently plagued by delays in their efforts to deliver new premium offerings — including increasing passenger demand for privacy, high-tech connectivity and inflight entertainment—to meet the surge in air travel.Flagship carriers including American, Lufthansa, Riyadh Air and Singapore Airlines are all struggling to navigate the lengthy, multi-year approval process for bespoke cabins.
How did we get to a place where seats are actually too fancy to fly in? It starts by rewinding the tape a few decades.
When the McCallister family dashes onto their flight to Paris in the 1990 film “Home Alone,” barely making it after an alarm clock failure, the parents — having waved their kids into coach — turn left into first class and settle into what were essentially comfortable, oversized recliners.
That was the standard for decades until British Airways introduced the world’s first lie-flat seat in 2000. In the decades since, front-row real estate has transformed into high-tech mini-apartments.
Take Lufthansa’s new premium Allegris suites and Senses, its sister carrier Swiss’ version. Both are a complete overhaul of their long-haul cabins, featuring seat heating, seat cooling and personal climate controls. Yet, as nice as those amenities are, every added feature introduces a fresh regulatory hurdle, in this case contributing to a multi-year delay before both airlines were able to deploy.
Experts estimate that certifying a new premium seat today takes at least six months longer than it did prior to the Covid pandemic, when lead times averaged one to two years.
Why reclining seats are vanishing from airplanes
“By the time you imagine it, design it, test it, get it certified, get it built — it is a lengthy three-year process,” Ben Minicucci, the CEO of Alaska Airlines, said in May on bringing the airline’s first-ever business-class suites to market. “We approved this design on a new product last year and now it’s getting the seat manufacturers aligned.”
Compounding the crisis is the fact that airlines are actively resisting standardization in a bid to outdo each other.
“Another industry that is in a booming ramp-up phase, you want to scale it — you would go for standardization,” said Mark Hiller, the CEO of seat manufacturer Recaro. Instead, airlines are insisting on custom designs to stand out. “The interest and need for differentiation … are driving the demand and really lead to bottlenecks in the industry.”
Federal regulators are also taking a much harder line on crash safety tests for custom setups. FAA Administrator Bryan BedfordtoldThe Wall Street Journal in May that the agency sees premium seats “that just don’t pass our human factors tests for impact.”
The obsession with privacy is a massive part of the problem.
“If you went back 10 years ago, there were very few walls in the business-class cabin and today there are a lot,” Andrew Nocella, chief commercial officer of United Airlines, commented earlier this year. “I do think that the evolution of the cabins has made [certification] very complicated.”
United seems to have found a way through the regulatory maze, launching its updated Polaris suites complete with privacy doors on Boeing 787s less than a year after unveiling them in 2025. Nocella says the company worked closely with safety inspectors and manufacturers.
But for most carriers, every added wall, higher door and high-tech widget is another tangle of testing and paperwork.
Modern suites aren’t just big chairs anymore. They are elaborate pieces of architecture packed with complex and heavy new inflight entertainment screens and seat textiles, which populate cabins more densely than ever before.As ZIM Aircraft Seating Group CEO Raffael Rogg points out, every custom material and hard barrier has implications for dynamic impact testing, flammability and crucial Head Injury Criteria safety ratings.
Airline forced to rebalance planes because first class seats are too heavy
Every link in the aviation chain — airlines, planemakers, seat suppliers and regulators — is eager to clear the logjam. No manufacturer wants a multimillion-dollar jet sitting on the tarmac awaiting chairs or flying across the Atlantic carrying ghost suites.
“How do you identify risk with the customers early on and push that risk upstream?” Stephanie Pope, the CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, recently commented about seat certification delays. “There’s nothing our engineers can’t solve, it’s more the time that it takes to solve, and if you’re finding it towards the end of the process that’s going to cause some delivery challenges.”
Part of the solution is fixing predictable design flaws — like ensuring flight attendants can actually see passengers over high privacy walls — early in the development process to avoid last-minute delays. The FAA says it is actively collaborating with international safety partners to streamline approvals, but seat executives warn that throwing extra staff at the problem may not be enough to catch up with market demand.
“In the certification,authorities [and] the seat suppliers are ramping up,” said Recaro CEO Mark Hiller. “On the other hand, all these improvements are somehow eaten up by the more demand we’re having.” In fact, Hiller warns, the bottleneck could get worse before it gets better.
The best passenger airplanes of all time — ranked by CNN’s top aviation expert
KLM is a case in point. In an effort to avoid custom-design traps, the Dutch carrier chose an off-the-shelf model from seat manufacturer Stelia that was already flying on sister airline Air France. Yet despite taking the safer route, KLM’s new A350 business suites remain blocked off, awaiting the green light from European regulators EASA, which KLM says is now using a “revised interpretation of regulatory requirements.”
Delays or not, the airline industry has no plans to turn its back on luxury.
“The complex interiors I don’t see going away,” Boeing’s Pope said. “I think that is the wave of the future.”
She joked: “Someday we’ll all have a shower next to our seat.”
Until then, passengers will just have to hope the seat itself gets certified first.

title: Teen charged with murder of mother and brother used ChatGPT to create ‘fantasy stories’ about killing family, officials say
description: A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said.
author: Karina Tsui, Rebekah Riess
content:
A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said.
A plea of not guilty was entered Thursday for Arjun Aravind, 17, on two counts of murder, two counts of assault and battery on a family or household member and other charges. His mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14, were found dead Tuesday in their home in Acton, some 20 miles northwest of Boston, prosecutorssaid.
Arjun Aravind “had recently been demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryantoldreporters Wednesday, citing the law enforcement investigation.
“He was engaged in the use of ChatGPT in creating fantasy stories, kind of the Gothic novel kind of stories, asking questions, creating characters, asking what about this, if this happened to that, and they seem to appear to relate to threats to his family not surviving,” Ryansaid.
A “heavily damaged bloody laptop,” and “a bent utensil, possible [sic] a knife with an orange handle” were found at the scene, a police report obtained byCNN affiliate WCVBindicated. Venkatesan’s and Siddharth’s causes of death are still pending, Ryan said.
Aravind over the past year had had behavior issues and his family had hidden knives from him, the teen’s father said, WCVB reported, citing police reports.
The teen did not realize his mother and brother were dead until after he was arrested, his defense attorney, Debra DeWitt, told WCVB. CNN has asked her for comment.
AI technology allegedly has been linked to other criminal acts, and Florida this springsuedChatGPT ownerOpenAI,allegingthe tool had “no parental oversight,” got minors addicted, caused users to lose “critical thinking skills,” helped mass shooters and encouraged suicide.
OpenAI believes minors “need significant protection” and has “put in place industry leading protections and policies,” it has said. CNN reached out Friday to OpenAI about this week’s murder case.
Aravind was ordered held without bail and to undergo a mental health evaluation. A probable cause hearing was set for September 11.
Florida sues OpenAI, alleging it’s unsafe for children
Policeresponded Tuesday to his family home after a tutor arrived for a scheduled visit and could not get in, Ryan said Wednesday in a news conference. The teen’s father was then notified and requested a wellness check.
Officers found the two victims inside – but not Aravind, who was believed to have fled using his mother’s 2014 green Honda Accord, she said. While responding to a separate incident Wednesday morning, police in neighboring Wayland found Aravind in his mother’s car in a parking lot and took him into custody.
The family had only recently moved to Acton for “better schools and support system for the kids,” DeWitt said.
“We put an enormous weight on our kids … We know the kids will be seeing and reading about this, likely on social media,” Ryan said. “This is an unspeakable tragedy. It is an incredibly dark day – obviously, an insurmountable tragedy for the dad in this case.”

title: Man who official says has past mental health issues faces hate crime charges after disrupting service at Manhattan synagogue
description: A man who a law enforcement official says has a history of mental health issues has been arrested and charged with multiple hate crimes after disrupting Shabbat services and injuring a woman at Central Synagogue in Manhattan Friday night, New York police said.
author: Mark Morales, Karina Tsui, Rebekah Riess
content:
A man who a law enforcement official says has a history of mental health issues has been arrested and charged with multiple hate crimes after disrupting Shabbat services and injuring a woman at Central Synagogue in Manhattan Friday night, New York police said.
The man, identified as 46-year-old Larry Montes from the Bronx, also “damaged synagogue property,” and spat at and headbutted a member of the synagogue’s security team as he was escorted out of the building, Commissioner Jessica Tischsaid on X.
Montes was arraigned Saturday night in criminal court, where a judge set bail at $10,000 cash and $30,000 in bonds, according to the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office. If convicted, Montes could face five to 15 years in prison, the DA said.
Congregants scrambled Friday night as shouts of panic erupted, according to a clip from the synagogue’s livestream obtained byCNN affiliate WCBS. A security guard restrained the man as he barreled down the aisle, according to WCBS.
Montes entered the synagogue during the service and was sitting down for roughly 10 minutes before he got up and was confronted by security, a law enforcement official told CNN.
Security officers began to question him once he started walking toward an area that wasn’t open to the public, prompting him to chop at two candles, each valued around $10,000, with his hands, the official said.
When he tried to make his way toward the rabbi, security escorted him out and he proceeded to attack a woman and the security guard while also yelling a racial slur at him, the official said.
A 63-year-old woman suffered a small cut to her lip and injuries to her right forearm after being struck by the man, an NYPD spokesperson told CNN.
The District Attorney’s office said it has requested full temporary orders of protection for the victims involved.
“He was screaming and yelling. I heard a loud pop … We thought it was a gun,” Susan Roane, who was at the service, told WCBS.
Congregant Arlynn Greenbaum told WCBS she saw the suspect wasn’t armed, but still wanted to take cover.
“He was just ranting and raving and yelling,” she said. “He was very full of hate.”
Montes has several sealed arrests, some of which were robberies, as well as a history of mental health issues, the law enforcement official told CNN. Investigators do not have evidence that he was targeting anyone inside the synagogue, the official said.
While the precise motivation for Friday’s attack remains unclear, it comes amid a rise in reports of antisemitic assaults on American soil. Just last year, the US reacheda record high of such attacks, including its first fatality since 2022, according to a report published by the Anti-Defamation League.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has had a tense relationship with some members of the city’s Jewish community over his fierce criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza, was quick to condemn the attack.
Antisemitic assaults reached a record high in the US last year, Anti-Defamation League report says
“This despicable act has no place in our city, and our administration will do everything in our power to keep Jewish New Yorkers safe,” he saidonX on Friday night. He added that New Yorkers must be able to observe their religion without fear of violence.
“I am grateful to Central Synagogue’s security team for swiftly stepping in to prevent more violence, and to the NYPD sergeant who apprehended him and took him into custody,” Mamdani said in a social media postannouncing Montes’ charges on Saturday.
“Our administration will always stand against bigotry in all its forms. We will use every tool at our disposal to confront antisemitism and keep Jewish New Yorkers — and all New Yorkers — safe,” the mayor added.
Montes has been charged with “two counts of assault as a hate crime and one count of criminal mischief as a hate crime, along with other charges,” Tisch said.
“I have spoken with the rabbi of the synagogue, and I’m relieved that no one was seriously injured. Those who were hurt were evaluated at the scene and are doing well,” Tisch said.
In a statement posted onFacebookhours after the attack, Central Synagogue said it was grateful for the outpouring of support after Friday’s “disturbing events.”
“We will keep on gathering for joyful, meaningful Judaism with our Central family every week,” the temple wrote.
“We went through something really hard and scary last night,” synagoguecantor Jenna Pearsallsaid, before offering a “healing prayer … focused on the whole community, on all of us,” during a Shabbat service Saturday morning.
Central Synagogue Rabbi Andrew Kaplan Mandelopened theserviceon Saturday by saying the congregation is grateful to be safe and won’t “allow anyone to rob us of our attention on Shabbat.”
“Our day of rest was interrupted last night by a security incident in our main sanctuary, but we are OK. We are safe. We are grateful to be here, we are grateful to our security team for supporting us. We feel so grateful for our community,” the rabbi said.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon condemned what he said was an antisemitic attack in a post directly criticizing the city’s leader.
“This is another chilling reminder that anti-Semitism does not belong in the past, it’s occurring here and now, in the heart of New York,” he wrote onX.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul called the attack “appalling.”
“Jewish New Yorkers have every right to worship openly, proudly, and without fear,”she wrote on X.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s David Williams, Emma Tucker and Tina Burnside contributed to this report.

title: A Kansas town will pay $850K to end a reporter’s lawsuit over a 2023 raid on her paper’s offices
description: A small Kansas town has agreed to pay $850,000 to former reporter Phyllis Zurn to end her federal lawsuit over a police raid of the paper’s offices in 2023.
author: Associated Press
content:
A small Kansas town has agreed to pay $850,000 to a former reporter at its weekly newspaper to end her federal lawsuit over apolice raidof the paper’s offices in 2023 that igniteda national furor over press freedom.
Now-retired Marion County Record reporter Phyllis Zorn said inher lawsuitthat the raid violated press freedoms and protections from unreasonable law enforcement searches guaranteed by the US Constitution. She also said it almost immediately led to health problems, causing the return of potentially life-threatening seizures that had been controlled for years with medication.
Zorn’s attorney, Randy Rathbun, and an attorney for the city Marion, Jennifer Hill, filed a joint statement Tuesday — the third anniversary of the raid on the newspaper’s offices — thatZorn’s lawsuitwas being dismissed. It was among the lawsuits filed in federal court against local officials over the raids of the newspaper’s offices, the home of publisher Eric Meyer and the home of a former City Council member.
Rathbun did not immediately return a phone message Wednesday seeking comment. Another attorney for the city, Scott Ufford, declined to comment about the settlement but confirmed the amount.
Marion Police Chief Gideon Cody said he was investigating whether the paper had committed identity theft or other crimes in accessing a local restaurant owner’s state driving record, but authorities who examined the raids said they werenot legally justified.Meyer, Zorn and others saw the raids as retaliation for hard-hitting local coverage and efforts to gather information about Cody’s past in law enforcement.
The raids put a national spotlight on Marion, a town of about 1,900 residents about 150 miles (241 kilometers) southwest of Kansas City, and Codylater resigned.Meyer’s 98-year-old-mother, also the paper’s co-owner, who lived with him,died the day afterthe raids, and he blames stress from the raid at their home for her death.
Marion County agreed in November to paya little more than $3 millionto parties in the five lawsuits, including $600,000 to Zorn, to settle claims against its officials. While some of the remaining legal claims against the city and past and present officials have been settled or dismissed, some still remain, and a pretrial Zoom hearing is scheduled for October 15.
Questions about Cody’s conduct after the state launched an investigation of the raid led two special prosecutors to file a felonyobstruction of justice chargeagainst him in state district court,allegingthat he persuaded a witness, the local restaurant owner, to withhold information from authorities. He pleaded not guilty, and a trial set for the end of this month has been postponed.

title: What comes next after Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal charges in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO
description: Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea to federal charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson raises questions about the future of his state murder trial.
author: Kara Scannell, Nicki Brown, Lauren del Valle
content:
More than a year after the fatal shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, 28-year-oldLuigi Mangione confessed to the killingin his own words as he pleaded guilty to federal charges in court Friday – a move that raises questions about the future of his upcoming state murder trial.
“On the morning of December 4, 2024,I shot Mr. Thompsonin Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said as he sat in a federal courtroom flanked by his defense attorneys. He spoke calmly – and expressed no remorse for murdering the 50-year-old healthcare executive and father of two as Thompson’s family members, including his widow, sat in the front row of the courtroom and held one another.
The change of plea is a stunning development in a case that has captured national attention and exposed deep-seated frustration with the American healthcare system, as Mangione amassed a horde of devoted followers who sympathized with his cause and held him up asa kind of folk hero.
Mangione faced both state and federal charges: His guilty plea staves off his federal trial on two stalking charges, which had been scheduled for January 2027. But the fate ofMangione’s state case, set to go to trial next month, now hangs in the balance as his attorneys seek to get second-degree murder and weapons charges dismissed over double jeopardy protections.
A legal showdown that will likely delay the state trial is sure to follow, as the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office signaled Friday it would fight to see its prosecution proceed.
Luigi Mangione’s defense team filed motions to dismiss state charges against him, arguing double jeopardy applies after Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. CNN’s Kara Scannell reports state prosecutors intend to fight and litigate against the motion.
Whether it does remains to be seen, but legal experts said Mangione’s defense has a strong argument that could see most of the state charges dismissed under New York state’sdouble jeopardylaw, which goes further than the US Constitution in prohibiting two prosecutions based on the same criminal act or conduct.
“I think it’s more likely than not that the state case goes away with the federal guilty plea,” said Anthony Capozzolo, a former prosecutor with the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office and a former federal prosecutor with the Eastern District of New York.
Capozzolo expects New York prosecutors will be blocked from moving ahead “because it’s likely both offenses will be punishing someone for the murder of the same victim and the elements of the federal and state cases are punishing the same harm or evil.”
“Therefore, the offenses will not be deemed different enough to allow New York to continue to prosecute the case,” he said.
Mangione’s guilty plea in the federal case came during a conference which was hastily scheduled hours after he appeared in state court earlier this week to discuss the upcoming trial. CNN reported this week Mangione’s defense attorneys were in plea negotiations with federal prosecutors – although his defense attorneys confirmed in court Friday no agreement was reached.
US Judge Margaret Garnett set Mangione’s sentencing forDecember 18. He faces a maximum sentence of life in prison; if the DA’s office is satisfied with his federal sentence, it could agree to dismiss the state charges.
For the first time Friday, Mangione publicly described Thompson’s killing in his own words, detailing the steps he took to plan the shooting outside a Midtown Manhattan hotel hosting UnitedHealthcare’s annual investor conference. Mangione spoke quickly, prompting the judge to interrupt him because she was having trouble hearing.
“After years of enduring severe pain from a broken back, navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others, I learned that UnitedHealthcare would be holding its annual investor conference in New York City on December 4, 2024,” Mangione said, adding the conference would be attended by investors and executives but not medical providers or patients.
Mangione used a 3D printer to create part of a firearm, he said, which he equipped with a silencer and magazine before travelling to New York City in November 2024.
“I then emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an investor at a firm managing over $50 billion in assets and requesting information about the conference,” Mangione said. “Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour.”
Reading a prepared statement with little emotion, Mangione described shooting Thompson: “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”
He did not look at Thompson’s family.
Thompson’s killing outside a Midtown Manhattan hotel ignited a multistate manhunt that ended five days later, when police in Altoona, Pennsylvania, arrested Mangione in a McDonald’s.
In his backpack, authorities said, they found a gun that linked him to the crime scene and a notebook that included writings about targeting the CEO at the “parasitic bean-counter convention” – strong evidence experts previously told CNN wouldnarrow his defense options at trial.
Mangione’s lawyers raised concerns when he was first charged in both jurisdictions that the 28-year-old was unfairly being tried twice for the same crime. Since then, the prospect of double jeopardy has remained an open question that’s come up several times during open court proceedings and in filings.
Manhunt: Tracking the CEO Murder Suspect
Immediately following the federal hearing Friday, Mangione’s defense team filed a motion asking New York Judge Gregory Carro to dismiss second-degree murder and weapons charges in his state case, Karen Friedman Agnifilo told reporters outside the federal courthouse Friday.
“It was a single tragic event, yet he’s being prosecuted twice for the same conduct,” she told reporters.
“Thankfully, New York law does not allow this,” Friedman Agnifilo said. “New York law does not permit a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime under a statute that governs successive prosecutions.”
In its filing, the defense asked the state judge to dismiss the charges, accusing federal and state prosecutors of coordinating their cases “to maximize the punitive effectiveness of the two cases at the expense of Mr. Mangione.”
Mangione’s defense claimed state and federal prosecutors cut a deal to allow the state case to proceed first in an effort to evade double jeopardy protections and give both offices an opportunity to prosecute Mangione, violating the killer’s constitutional rights.
“This coordinated deal between them had a specific purpose: The scheme was designed solely to ensure dual successive prosecutions, in order to attempt to avoid double jeopardy protections,” the filing said.
The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office acknowledged Mangione’s motion to dismiss the state charges Friday afternoon but said it was ready to fight for its case in court.
“We are encouraged that Mr. Thompson’s family received a measure of accountability today. While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan D.A.’s Office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family,” a spokesperson said.
Carro now must consider whether to allow the trial to move forward on all eight charges Mangione presently faces in the indictment. He could delay the September 8 start of jury selection while the parties argue in court filings – or even wait for the federal sentencing to play out before deciding.
Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty Friday to federal stalking charges, telling the court he posed as an investor to obtain information about UnitedHealthcare’s 2024 conference, which CEO Brian Thompson was scheduled to attend. “I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said during his allocution to the court. “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”
Either side could appeal Carro’s decision, which would likely further delay a possible state trial – if it proceeds at all.
New York legal experts have suggested state prosecutors are unlikely to see a trial against Mangione now that he’s resolved the federal case.
“I do believe that based upon the law that the state trial goes away. I do think that this double jeopardy argument is real,” CNN legal analyst and criminal defense attorney Joey Jackson said, because both cases involve “the same sort of transaction and occurrence, the same set of facts,” and the same “evil” that is “eradicated” by Mangione’s plea Friday.
Stacy Schneider, a New York City criminal defense attorney, told CNN’s Jake Tapper Mangione’s defense has a “calculated, good shot” at getting the state case dismissed, “but not a slam dunk.”
“They want to invoke the New York state double jeopardy law, which is a broad law, and says not only can you not prosecute them for the same act – but you can’t prosecute them for the same act or criminal transaction, even though it’s two different offenses,” she said.
Prosecutors, meanwhile, will likely argue “the act of stalking was a prelude to the murder,” Schneider said, and that the acts encompassed by the federal charges are “not the same as actually pulling the trigger.”
Whatever happens with the state case, experts said, Mangione will also likely be looking ahead to his sentencing in December, when he will have another opportunity to address the court.
His attorneys will likely present what’s known as mitigating evidence, which the judge would weigh in determining his sentence.
After Friday’s court appearance, Mangione’s defense attorney said Mangione has “accepted full responsibility” for Thompson’s death, calling Friday a “solemn and significant day.”
“As Luigi explained in court today, he endured years of severe, debilitating pain following a broken back while struggling to navigate our healthcare and health insurance systems,” Friedman Agnifilo said outside the courthouse. “Like the thousands of people who have reached out since this tragedy to share their own experiences, he believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.”
In a statement, Thompson’s family called the guilty plea “an important step toward justice,” and noted Mangione’s pending cases in New York and Pennsylvania state court. The latter case involves charges stemming from his arrest.
“While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable,” the Thompson family said in their statement. “Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime.”
CNN’s August Phillips contributed to this report.

title: Suspect in Virginia State University shooting is arrested after police find him hiding in a closet
description: Police arrested a 19-year-old found hiding in a dormitory closet at Virginia State University on Saturday in connection with an overnight shooting on campus that left five people wounded, including one with critical injuries.
author: Associated Press
content:
Police arrested a 19-year-old found hiding in a dormitory closet at Virginia State University on Saturday in connection with an overnight shooting on campus that left five people wounded, including one with critical injuries.
Camron Harris of Henrico, Virginia, is not a student on campus nor were four of the people injured, Chesterfield County Police said in a statement. They ranged in age from 17 to 23. One of the injured, a 20-year-old, is a student and has been released from the hospital, authorities said. The victims’ names have not been released.
Authorities have given no information about a possible motive. Police obtained eight felony warrants for Harris, including for malicious wounding and the use of a firearm in the commission of a felony. It wasn’t immediately clear whether he had an attorney who could speak on his behalf.
The university said in an earlier statement that authorities were searching for multiple suspects, but police provided no additional information Saturday evening about the search. University officials said earlier in the day that law enforcement did not believe there was an immediate threat to the campus community, and a campus lockdown had been lifted.
The shooting, just after 1:30 a.m. Saturday, prompted a campus lockdown and came as students were getting ready for the new school year.
It happened near the university’s Quad Annexes, where campus police and Chesterfield County officers discovered five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories.
According to the university’s website, residence halls opened for students a week ago, and classes resume on Monday. Many students had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students.
“We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends, and the broader VSU community,” the university statement said. “The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority.”
The campus had a large law enforcement presence on Saturday morning, and the university informed students that they should monitor their email for additional safety measures and information about support services. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office were assisting, county police said.
Virginia State University is a historically Black university located in Ettrick, Virginia, about 24 miles (39 kilometers) south of the state capital of Richmond. The public university has about 5,700 students and was the first fully state-supported four-year college for Black Americans. Most of its students are undergraduates.
The university has grown in recent years while attempting to improve safety and retain its historic charm, said Arthur Fridrich, the university’s former director of distance education, who lives near the campus and visits regularly. A shooting like this just as students return for classes is heartbreaking for the community, he said.
“To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students, and for some it will be difficult to rid their minds of this term,” Fridrich said. “For those that were shot, my heart bleeds. I hope that they all mend and somehow do not let this event define their lives.”

title: 1 dead, thousands without power as Tropical Storm Lala lashes Hawaii
description: One person is dead and tens of thousands have lost power after Hurricane Lala lashed parts of Hawaii overnight, before weakening slightly Sunday morning to a tropical storm with 70 mph sustained winds and heavy rain.
author: Dalia Faheid, Karina Tsui, Chris Boyette, Tyler Ory, Dakota Smith
content:
One person is dead and tens of thousands have lost power after Hurricane Lala moved past parts of Hawaii overnight, before weakening slightly Sunday morning to a tropical storm with 70 mph sustainedwinds and heavy rain.
Nearly 130,000 customers are without power across the islands. Nearly 70% of the Big Island is without power. Hurricane-force wind gusts were reported in Hawaii, Honolulu and Maui counties, with the mountainous island terrain amplifying winds at higher elevations.
The island of Oahu, including the state’s capital Honolulu, is under a flash flood warning Sunday morning. Parts of Hawaii’s Big Island are also under a flash flood warning, and National Weather Service hadpreviously calledthat warning a “Particularly Dangerous Situation.”
“Several occupied homes may have been swept off their foundations, and based on that, civil defense has initiated a search and rescue mission,” Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alamedasaidovernight.
Lala was starting to pull away from the islands Sunday morning, but heavy rain is expected to continue throughout the day across the island chain.
One person was killed in a storm-related car accident, Hawaii Gov. Josh Greensaid Saturday evening, while at least 19 buildings had lost their roofs.
In avideo updateSaturday night, Hawaii County’s Acting Civil Defense Administrator Darryl Oliviera said occupants of a vehicle stuck in floodwaters were being rescued, though he did not provide further details.
Lala, which strengthened to a Category 1 storm Saturday, made its closest approach to Hawaii’s Big Island at around 5 p.m. local time, with its eyewall brushing the southern portion from roughly 30 miles away, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Videos obtained by CNN show streets flooded by torrential rainfall on the Big Island, which got over 30 inches of rain. More than 190 flights in and out of Hawaii have been postponed, Green said.
Emergency responders are expected to be busy dealing with urgent matters for 36 hours as the storm passes Hawaii, with damage assessment expected to begin on Monday, the governor said.
A record number of road closures and prolonged power outages had been reported, according to Mayor Alameda.
As Lala moves west, its most serious threat is its torrential rain,which could also spur additionalflash flooding across the other Hawaiian Islands. The National Hurricane Center warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain.
Up to 8 inches of additional rain is expected in parts of Kauai, where tropical storm warnings are in effect. Maui, Lanai, Molokai,Oahuand Kahoolawe are also under a tropical storm warning.
Waves could reach 8 to 12 feet, particularly on east-facing shores where a high surf advisory is in effect.
Landfalls — when the center of the eye moves over land — on the Hawaiian islands have happened only a handful of times in the modern record. The last tropical system to make landfall wasTropical Storm Olivia in 2018, which came ashore on Maui, the island’s first landfall since recordkeeping began in the 1950s.
The last landfalling hurricane was in 1992 whenCategory 4 Iniki hit Kauai, becoming the strongest storm to directly strike the state on record.
Across Hawaii, residents evacuated to designated shelters and scoured packed grocery stores as officials across several counties announced closures and prepared for potential landfall.
In Hilo, grocery stores and gas stations were busy as people stocked up on essentials,CNN affiliate Hawaii News Nowreported. Hawaii County was also offering sandbags for residents around the island. Around 130 people had fled to shelters Saturday, according to themayor.
“You got to take all the necessary precautions, right? So it’s batteries. It’s get your emergency kit, inform your neighbors, the kupuna (elders),” Mayor Alameda said earlier in the day. “Make sure that everybody’s safe because our island’s big and we have small communities and we’re very connected.”
Hawaii resident Maxine Totty-Hefley said living through the first hurricane in decades on the island is “really surreal” and described a mad dash at the grocery store Friday.
“Seeing people, like, rush through and getting their food and stock up on stuff. Like, lanterns were out, toilet paper was almost out,” she toldCNN affiliate KITV.
Totty-Hefley was planning to evacuate to higher ground with her pets, she said.
“We are going to pack up all the dogs and the dog food and everything, take it to my mom’s friend’s house,” she told KITV.
Many roads in Hawaii County are closed due to downed trees and utility lines and landslides, according to the County of Hawaii Mayor’s Office.
“While road crews are working hard to clear debris as conditions allow, we need all residents and visitors to heed all warnings, move into safe shelter, and stay off the roadways,” Alameda said.
County officials and the National Guard had also been discussing placing resources ahead of time in areashard-hit by stormsearlier this year, according to Hawaii News Now.
And in Oahu, officials opened eight hurricane refuge areas as public facilities like the Honolulu Zoo shuttered.
Officials urged residents to be cautious as the hurricane approached.
“We also need our community to do its part by securing property, checking emergency supplies, staying informed, and avoiding unnecessary travel and outdoor activities as conditions deteriorate,” Kauai Mayor Derek S.K. Kawakami said.
In Maui, temporary evacuation points were opened as county facilities closed, events were canceled and first responders prepared for impacts.
Tropical storms approaching Hawaii typically hit cooler ocean temperatures before reaching the islands, but Lala will remain over warmer waters due to an ongoing marine heatwave that extends to California and adeveloping Super El Niño.
El Niño is helping fuel increased storm potential in the central Pacific this year with warmer ocean temperatures and weaker winds in the upper atmosphere, which can normally break up storms.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast an above-average central Pacific season, with five to 13 cyclones expected.
CNN’s Andrew Freedman, Nic F. Anderson and Amanda Jackson contributed to this report.
